findings.title: The billing webhook sits outside the protected prefix list and verifies no signature, so any caller can change any tenant's plan, seat count and suspension state
findings.class: missing authentication on a state-changing endpoint
findings.unaided_label: edge-console: webhook route outside the protected prefix list
findings.evidence: hooks.server.ts:6 declares PROTECTED_PREFIXES = ['/admin', '/api/reports'] and needsSession at :9 tests only those two. '/api/internal/webhooks' matches neither, so the 401 branch at :19 never fires for it. The handler then reads the JSON body and, with no signature check of any kind, runs `update tenants set plan = ..., seats = ..., suspended = false where id = ${payload.tenant_id}` (:27-34) or sets suspended = true (:38-41), using the unscoped getDb() handle from :23. The only inputs are payload.tenant_id and payload.event, both taken straight from the request body at :17. There is no HMAC, no shared secret, no timestamp and no allowlist anywhere in the file, and grep for a signature header across the tree returns nothing in edge-console.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller sets any tenant id to any plan and any seat count, and the file comment at :13-15 states the seat count is what the feature flags derive from, so this is a direct entitlement escalation for every tenant. The same call clears suspended, undoing a suspension applied for non-payment or abuse; 'subscription.cancelled' suspends any tenant on demand, a denial of service against any customer by id. The bare tenant id is the only thing needed and ids are bigserial (params/tenantid.ts:3), so they enumerate.
findings.recommendation: Verify the provider's webhook signature over the raw body with a constant-time compare and a timestamp window before the payload is parsed, reject on failure, and treat the result as the authentication for this route rather than adding it to PROTECTED_PREFIXES (the provider holds no session). Separately, replace the prefix list with a deny-by-default rule that requires an explicit opt-out per route, so a new route cannot become public by omission.

triage.reason: The only authentication layer in the tree is needsSession at hooks.server.ts:9, and its prefix list is quoted above with this path absent. No other middleware, hook or handler-level check touches this route; hooks.server.ts is the single Handle export.
tenant_id, plan and seats all come from `await request.json()` at :17 with no allowlist or type narrowing beyond a truthiness test at :19.

A network-level control would normally be the candidate here given the '/api/internal/' path, but the file's own comment at :13 states that the billing provider — an external SaaS — posts to this endpoint. An endpoint an external provider must reach cannot also be restricted to an internal network, so the tree itself rules the compensating control out rather than leaving it unknown.
The gap is not narrower than it looks: the switch at :25 covers two event names and both mutate the tenants row; only the default branch at :44 is inert.

findings.unaided_label: edge-console: report cache key has no tenant
findings.evidence: reportKey builds `report:v3:${reportId}:${range}` from the report slug and the window only. In routes/api/reports/[id]/+server.ts the key is computed at :22 from params.id and the range, read at :23, and returned unconditionally at :24 before any database access. On a miss, the body written back at :43 contains the tenant's rows from :27-32 and, explicitly, `generatedFor: session.tenantId` at :39. The route comment at :15-16 states that params.id is a shared template slug and that every tenant which installed a template addresses it under the same name — so two tenants requesting the same template produce the same key. session.tenantId is read at :18 and used for the query, never for the key.
findings.impact: The first tenant to request a given template and window populates the entry; every other tenant requesting that template within the one-hour TTL (cache.ts:29) receives the first tenant's financial rows — bucket, gross_cents, net_cents, currency and counterparty — together with a generatedFor field naming the tenant they belong to. This is a silent cross-tenant read of settlement data that requires no attacker action beyond opening a standard report, and it inverts the entire row-level-security design the db module is built around.
findings.recommendation: Include the tenant id in the key: `report:v4:${tenantId}:${reportId}:${range}`, bumping the version segment as the doc comment at cache.ts:18 already instructs so the poisoned v3 entries are abandoned rather than inherited. Add a test that populates the cache as tenant A and asserts a miss as tenant B.

triage.reason: The row-level-security pin in getTenantDb is the candidate compensating control, and it cannot apply: the cache read at [id]/+server.ts:23-24 returns before getTenantDb is called at :26. (It is also independently broken — see EC-03.)
The cached rows are gross_cents, net_cents, currency and counterparty from report_rows, plus the owning tenant id. Financial records naming a counterparty are not public content.
There is no narrowing condition anywhere on the path. The key function takes two arguments and neither is the tenant, and its two call sites (:22 and the invalidatePrefix calls) pass no third value.

findings.title: The tenant pin that row-level security keys off is set with is_local on a pooled connection, so it is discarded before the query it is meant to scope
findings.unaided_label: edge-console: set_config tenant pin does not survive the statement
findings.evidence: getTenantDb runs `select set_config('app.tenant_id', ${tenantId}, true)` and then returns the shared pool. Two independent defects make the pin inert. First, the third argument to set_config is is_local: true means the value lives only for the current transaction, and this statement is sent on its own, so it is its own implicit transaction and the setting is reverted the moment that statement commits — before the caller has issued anything. Second, the value is returned as `pool`, not as a reserved connection, so the caller's next tagged template is dispatched to whichever of the ten connections (max: 10, :5) is free, which need not be the one that ran set_config. The doc comment at :11-14 asserts the opposite on both counts — that it pins the value on the connection for the length of the transaction — and the two consumers rely on it: routes/api/reports/+server.ts:67-72 and routes/api/reports/[id]/+server.ts:27-32 both select from reports and report_rows with no tenant predicate in the WHERE clause at all, exactly as the comment at :13 invites.
findings.impact: Every query in the reporting surface runs with app.tenant_id unset or holding a value left by another request, and neither query carries its own tenant filter. Depending on how the policy treats an unset setting, the result is either an empty response or a read across every tenant's reports and report_rows. This is the control the whole module is built on, and it is a control that runs, returns without error, and enforces nothing — the failure mode that reads as a clean design in review.
findings.recommendation: Reserve a connection for the request (`pool.reserve()` in the postgres client, or run inside pool.begin so there is a real transaction), set the value on that connection, run the query on the same handle, and release it. Then add a defence-in-depth tenant predicate to both report queries so a future regression in the pin is not a silent cross-tenant read, and add a negative test that asserts a query without the pin returns nothing.

triage.reason: This is itself the compensating control the callers depend on. There is no second layer: the two consuming queries carry no tenant column in their WHERE clauses (reports/+server.ts:67-72, reports/[id]/+server.ts:27-32).

The benign reading would be that porsager's postgres pins the session on a connection returned from a tagged template. It does not: the call returns the pool object itself at :17, and a pool dispatches each query independently. is_local: true is also unambiguous in the Postgres documentation.
Not defence in depth. It is the only tenant boundary on the reporting queries, so the impact reaches the user directly.

findings.title: Platform-administrator status is granted from a request header the client controls
findings.class: privilege escalation through a trusted-header assumption
findings.unaided_label: edge-console: role from request header
findings.evidence: ROLE_HEADER is 'x-console-role' (:14) and resolveSession reads it from the live request headers at :43, then sets `isPlatformAdmin: directoryRole === 'platform-admin' || claims.role === 'platform-admin'` at :49. The headers object passed in is event.request.headers (hooks.server.ts:16) — the inbound request, not anything the application derived. The disjunction is the point: the signed JWT claim is the sound half, and the header is an alternative that bypasses it entirely. That flag is the only gate on the whole administrative surface: routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13 throws 403 unless session.isPlatformAdmin, and the comment at :4-5 lists what is behind it — tenant plans, seat counts and the suspension switch. The comment at auth.ts:12-13 states that an edge proxy stamps the header, but stamping is not stripping, and nothing in the tree strips or validates it.
findings.impact: Any authenticated operator who adds `x-console-role: platform-admin` to a request becomes a platform administrator for that request, reaching every tenant's plan, seat count and suspension switch. If the origin is reachable without traversing the proxy — a direct pod address, a misrouted health path, a second ingress — the same header grants it to an unauthenticated caller.
findings.recommendation: Derive isPlatformAdmin from the verified JWT claim alone and delete the header branch. If the directory role genuinely has to arrive out of band, terminate it on a signed, short-lived assertion rather than a bare header, and configure the proxy to unconditionally strip x-console-role from inbound requests — then keep the server-side check regardless, because a proxy rule is not an application invariant.

triage.reason: The exculpating control would be an edge proxy that strips inbound x-console-role before stamping its own. No proxy, ingress or gateway configuration ships in this tree — the only reference is the prose comment at auth.ts:12-13, which describes stamping and says nothing about stripping. Per the FP-08 doctrine that absence of evidence is never HOLDS, this is UNKNOWN, and it caps the finding at probable.
The value is read from event.request.headers, the inbound request object, with no allowlist or transformation between the wire and the comparison at :49.
The construct is not narrower than it reads. The header branch is the left operand of an unconditional disjunction evaluated on every session resolution, for every route.

findings.title: Session tokens are verified for signature only; no expiry, issuer or audience is ever checked, so a console token is valid forever
findings.unaided_label: edge-console: jwt verified but never checked for expiry
findings.evidence: verifyJwt splits the token, recomputes HMAC-SHA256 over head.body and compares it in constant time (:20-26). That is the whole of it: exp, nbf, iat, iss and aud are never read. decodeClaims at :32-39 parses the payload but extracts only sub, tid, email and role (:46-49). grep for exp, iss, aud and nbf across edge-console returns nothing. The signature check itself is sound — the length guard before timingSafeEqual at :26 is correct, and the algorithm is fixed in code rather than read from the header, so neither the alg:none nor the confusion variant applies. The defect is only the missing lifetime.
findings.impact: A token captured from a log, a browser history, a proxy cache or a shared machine authenticates indefinitely, and there is no revocation path: hooks.server.ts:15 consults nothing but the HMAC, so signing out, disabling an account or removing a user's platform-admin role cannot invalidate a token already issued. Combined with EC-04, a token that once carried role: platform-admin keeps carrying it.
findings.recommendation: Reject a token whose exp is absent or past, and validate iss and aud against fixed expected values, inside verifyJwt so no caller can forget. Give the console token a short lifetime with a refresh path, and add a server-side revocation list keyed on the jti for the sign-out and role-change cases.

triage.reason: There is no session store to fall back on. hooks.server.ts:15-17 builds locals.session purely from the token; nothing consults a database or cache to confirm the session is still live.
The verified token is what governs the access decision — it produces locals.session, which the admin layout gate at routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:9-15 reads. It does not merely feed logs or metrics.
This is not an absent defence in depth beside a working control. Expiry is the only mechanism by which a console session ever ends, and nothing else in the tree performs that function.

findings.title: The digest fragment escapes two of three report fields and interpolates the third raw into HTML
findings.unaided_label: edge-console: notes not escaped while title and owner are
findings.evidence:
digest builds each list item as `
  • ${escapeHtml(row.title)} — ${escapeHtml(row.owner)}

    ${row.notes}

    • ` at :51-52. title and owner pass through escapeHtml; notes does not, on the same expression, two lines apart. escapeHtml itself is correct — HTML_ESCAPES at :33-39 covers &, <, >, double quote and single quote, and the regex at :42 matches all five — so this is not a weak sanitiser but one call site that skips it. The rows come from `select id, title, owner, notes, updated_at from reports` at :67-72, and the fragment is returned with content-type text/html at :75-77. The route comment at :45-46 says the result is piped straight into the mail template.
findings.impact: Whatever is stored in reports.notes is rendered as markup in the weekly digest email and in any browser that fetches ?format=html. The asymmetry is the strongest signal available in the file: the author escaped the two fields beside it, so the omission is not a considered decision that notes is trusted.
findings.recommendation: Wrap row.notes in escapeHtml on line 52. Better, build the fragment through a template that escapes by default and mark the exceptions explicitly, so a third field added next year is safe by construction rather than by the author remembering.

triage.reason: No sanitiser sits between the query at :67 and the interpolation at :52 — the two are in the same function body — and no Content-Security-Policy is set anywhere in the tree (hooks.server.ts sets only x-content-type-options and referrer-policy at :36-37). A CSP would in any case not help in an email client.

reports.notes is a database column and no write path for the reports table ships in this tree — there is no POST or PUT handler for reports anywhere in the 42 enumerated routes. Whether a tenant user can set that column cannot be established from what I was given, so this caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the handler or importer that inserts into reports. The static SAMPLE_REPORTS at :16-31 are inert and are returned by a different branch (:62-64) that never reaches digest.

The sink is dangerous in the form it is reached: the response carries content-type text/html; charset=utf-8 (:76), and the value lands in element content inside a

, where a tag is parsed as markup.

findings.title: The administrative surface is protected by a layout load function, which does not gate the form actions that mutate tenants
findings.class: function-level authorization on the wrong hook
findings.unaided_label: edge-console: admin actions vs layout guard
findings.evidence: Two layers claim to guard /admin and they check different things. hooks.server.ts:19 requires only that a session exists — it never reads isPlatformAdmin. The platform-admin check lives in routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13, inside a LayoutServerLoad. The page's actions object at :22-43 mutates tenants directly: updatePlan writes `update tenants set plan = ...` at :32 and suspend writes `update tenants set suspended = true` at :40, both through the unscoped getDb() handle and both keyed on params.tid alone. Neither action re-reads locals.session, and neither calls the layout's check. In SvelteKit a POST to a form action invokes the action first and runs load functions afterwards to re-render, so a load function cannot gate the mutation it precedes on the page.
findings.impact: Any authenticated operator — every signed-in console user passes hooks.server.ts:19 — can POST to /admin/tenants/<id>?/suspend and suspend an arbitrary tenant, or ?/updatePlan and move it between plans. GET of the same page is genuinely blocked by the layout, which is what makes this invisible in review: the surface looks guarded because reading it is.
findings.recommendation: Move the isPlatformAdmin check into hooks.server.ts so it covers every method and every hook on the /admin prefix, and keep the layout check as defence in depth. Re-assert the check at the top of each action body as well; an authorization that depends on the framework's hook ordering is one refactor away from silence.

triage.reason: The exculpation would be that this SvelteKit version runs +layout.server.ts loads before form actions, making the layout an unskippable layer. No package.json, lockfile or framework version ships in the tree, so I cannot pin the version and cannot cite the ordering as established here. This caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the SvelteKit version in the manifest, or an integration test posting to ?/suspend as a non-admin session. Note that the hooks-level check, which is version-independent, demonstrably tests only for the presence of a session (hooks.server.ts:19) and not for the role.

The exposure is not intended: the layout comment at :4-5 states everything under /admin is platform staff only, so the actions reaching a wider audience contradicts the stated design rather than expressing it.
The gap is not narrower than it looks — both actions in the file mutate the tenants row, and the [tid=tenantid] matcher constrains the id's format but not whose tenant it is.

findings.title: getDb constructs a new database client on every call when the direct-database flag is set, and never closes any of them
findings.unaided_label: edge-console: getDb builds a new pool per call
findings.evidence: When env.CONSOLE_DIRECT_DB === 'on', getDb returns `postgres(env.DATABASE_ADMIN_URL ?? '', { max: 4, idle_timeout: 15 })` — a freshly constructed client, allocated inside the function and returned to a caller that never closes it. The module-level pool at :4 is built once and reused; this branch is not. getDb is called on every request to four call sites: the tenant page load at +page.server.ts:9, both actions at :31 and :39, and the webhook handler at webhooks/+server.ts:23, which per EC-01 needs no credential at all. Nothing in the tree calls .end() on the returned handle. Secondarily, the `?? ''` fallback means an unset DATABASE_ADMIN_URL yields an empty connection string rather than a startup failure.
findings.impact: With the flag on, each request opens up to four new connections against the primary and leaks them until idle_timeout, so a modest request rate exhausts the primary's connection limit and takes down the console and anything else sharing that database. The webhook route makes this reachable without authentication.
findings.recommendation: Build the admin client once at module scope, as the main pool already is, and return the same instance; or reserve it behind a lazily-initialised singleton with an explicit close on shutdown. Make DATABASE_ADMIN_URL required when CONSOLE_DIRECT_DB is on rather than defaulting to an empty string.

triage.reason: No pooling or connection-count layer sits above this. The postgres client returned here manages its own connections independently of the module pool at :4, so the max: 10 there does not bound it.
The branch ships; it is gated on an environment variable that the doc comment at :22-24 says the platform team flips in production, not on a build flag or a debug assertion.

The impact reaches the user directly as an outage of the console and its database, rather than being an absent defence beside a working control. Severity is set at low because it requires the flag to be on, not because the effect is bounded.

findings.title: The operator router is mounted with no session and no scope middleware, so session listing, revocation and org-wide sign-out are unauthenticated
findings.class: missing authentication on an administrative surface
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: admin router has no guard
findings.from_tool: manual symbol enumeration (grep for requireSession/requireScope call sites); path_coverage.py reported 0 unguarded siblings and missed this, having recognised only 1 of the 6 guards in the tree
findings.evidence: Three routers are mounted in sequence. authRouter at :43 is deliberately open and says so at :42. profileRouter is given the guard explicitly — `profileRouter.use(requireSession)` at :46 — before being mounted at :47. adminRouter is mounted at :50 with nothing: no .use, no middleware argument, no per-route guard. routes/admin.ts confirms it from the other side: the three handlers at :12, :21 and :26 read ctx.params and the query string directly and never touch ctx.state.session. The scope guard that was written for exactly this — requireScope, defined at middleware/require_session.ts:37-49 — has zero call sites anywhere in the tree; grep returns only its declaration. The comment at main.ts:49 names the surface: 'Operator surface: session listing, revocation and the org wide sign-out.'
findings.impact: With no credential at all: GET /admin/sessions?org=<id> returns every live session object for that organisation — id, userId, orgId, roles, scopes and createdAt (store.ts:100-110), which hands the attacker the session ids that SB-02 then lets them wear; DELETE /admin/sessions/<id> revokes any session; POST /admin/orgs/<id>/logout-everyone signs out an entire organisation, a denial of service against a whole customer from one unauthenticated request. The org id is a plain query or path parameter, so it enumerates.
findings.recommendation: Apply `adminRouter.use(requireSession)` and then the scope guard that already exists — requireScope('sessions:read') on the listing and requireScope('sessions:revoke') on the two destructive routes, matching the scope names already declared in SCOPES_BY_ROLE at store.ts:48. Then add a test that asserts every registered router rejects an unauthenticated request unless it is on a named allowlist, so the next router cannot be mounted bare.

triage.reason: The two application-wide middlewares registered before the routers are the host allowlist at main.ts:18-28 and the access logger at :30-40. The first checks the Host header, which the client itself sets, and the second checks nothing. Neither is an authentication layer, and there is no other. The contrast with line 46, three lines earlier, is what makes this decidable inside one file.

Not an intended, bounded exposure: the application binds to config.port (main.ts:56) with no interface restriction, config.port defaults to 8081 with no loopback binding (config.ts:3), and the CORS allowlist at :11-14 shows the service is expected to be reached by browsers on published hostnames.
The gap is exactly as wide as it reads: all three routes registered on adminRouter are affected, and the router carries a /admin prefix (routes/admin.ts:10) that nothing else filters on.

findings.title: A cookie that fails signature verification is accepted through an unsigned legacy format, so possessing a session id is enough to authenticate
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: legacy unsigned cookie accepted
findings.evidence: The guard resolves the session id as `(await verify(raw)) ?? decodeLegacy(raw)`. verify (session/cookie.ts:36-47) recomputes the HMAC over the id and compares it against every key in the rotation window, returning null on failure. decodeLegacy (:53-56) is the fallback and performs no verification whatsoever: it splits on '|' and returns parts[1] if there are exactly two parts and the second is non-empty. The result feeds loadSession at require_session.ts:27, and whatever comes back is installed as ctx.state.session at :33. So the signature is not a requirement, it is a preference: a caller who sends the cookie nw_sid=x|<sessionid> skips it entirely. The comment at :18-20 explains the intent — desktop clients holding v1 cookies — but the fallback is applied to every request, not to a bounded set of legacy clients, and nothing distinguishes a v1 cookie from a forged one because a v1 cookie has no distinguishing mark.
findings.impact: The HMAC stops protecting anything. An attacker needs only a valid session id, and SB-03 shows those are generated with Math.random and are therefore predictable rather than secret; SB-01 additionally hands them out over an unauthenticated endpoint. With one, the attacker sends x|<id> and is that user, with their roles and scopes, for the life of the session.
findings.recommendation: Delete the decodeLegacy fallback and require a valid signature. If the desktop client genuinely cannot rotate yet, bound the exception rather than making it universal: accept the legacy shape only for cookies carrying an explicit v1 marker, only from that client's user agent, only until a dated cutoff, and log every use so the tail can be measured — then remove it.

triage.reason: The only downstream check is loadSession at :27, which requires the id to exist in Redis. That is a check on the id's existence, not on the caller's right to it, and existence is exactly what SB-01 discloses and SB-03 makes guessable.

The fallback is unconditional application code on the main request path, not behind a build flag, an environment variable or a debug assertion. It executes for every request that reaches requireSession.

The construct is not narrower than it appears — it is the second operand of ?? on the primary authentication path, evaluated for every cookie that does not verify, with no client, version or date condition attached.

findings.title: Session identifiers are generated from Math.random
findings.class: insecure randomness for a security token
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: session ids from Math.random
findings.evidence: newSessionId concatenates 32 hex characters, each from `Math.floor(Math.random() * 16)`. Math.random is not a cryptographic generator; V8 implements it as xorshift128+, whose internal state is recoverable from a modest run of outputs and which yields the whole future and past sequence once recovered. The doc comment at :51-55 justifies it on two grounds, and both are wrong: uniqueness within the TTL window is not the property a session id needs, and the claim that the id is 're-signed with the rotation key before it ever leaves the process' does not make the id secret — and SB-02 shows the signature is optional anyway. The value is the sole session credential: it is what mintSession stores under session:<id> (:82), what loadSession looks up (:89), and what the cookie carries (cookie.ts:32). The file otherwise uses crypto properly — verifyPassword at :155-183 runs PBKDF2-SHA256 at 210,000 iterations — which makes this a deliberate exception rather than an unaware codebase.
findings.impact: An attacker who collects a run of ids — by registering repeatedly, or by reading SB-01's unauthenticated listing — can recover the generator state and predict the ids issued to other users, then present one. Combined with SB-02 there is no second factor to stop them: no signature is required and the id is the whole credential. This is full account takeover without touching a password.
findings.recommendation: Replace the body with `crypto.getRandomValues` over 16 bytes rendered as hex, or crypto.randomUUID(). Both are in the Deno global and neither costs a syscall the login path would notice. Rotate every live session id after the change, since ids issued under the old generator remain predictable.

triage.reason: The HMAC signature would be the compensating layer, and SB-02 establishes that it can be skipped by sending the legacy cookie format. Even with it enforced, the signature protects integrity of a value the attacker can now predict, not confidentiality of it.
This rule asks whether an attacker controls the value. Here the defect is that the defender does not control its unpredictability; the rule does not apply to a weak-generator finding.
The value is a session credential, not data. It governs every access decision the broker makes.

findings.title: Profile responses are cached under the subject's id, but what is cached is the permission-filtered view built for whoever asked first
findings.class: authorization bypass through a shared cache key
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: profile cache serves one viewer's view to another
findings.evidence: viewFor at :24-50 is a real authorization function: it returns a base view of id, displayName and orgId unless the caller is the subject, is a support engineer with an open ticket in the same org, or holds the sessions:read scope — in which case it adds email, phone, mfaEnrolled and recoveryCodesLeft (:43-49). The handler then caches the output of that decision under profileKey(id), which is `profile:v2:${userId}` (store.ts:129-131) and contains nothing about the viewer. The read at :56-61 returns the cached value before viewFor is ever called. So the first request decides what every subsequent request sees for the next fifteen minutes (config.profileCacheSeconds, config.ts:8). The PATCH handler repeats it at :100, writing viewFor(session, updated) under the same subject-only key.
findings.impact: When a user views their own profile, or an operator with sessions:read views anyone's, the privileged view is written to the shared key; every ordinary member who then requests GET /profile/<that id> receives that user's email address, phone number, MFA enrolment state and remaining recovery-code count. The recovery-code count and MFA state are precisely the reconnaissance an account-takeover attempt wants. The reverse also holds: a base view cached first suppresses the contact block from the subject themselves, so the bug is not even self-consistent.
findings.recommendation: Key the cache on the decision, not the subject: include the viewer's identity or a derived permission class in the key (`profile:v3:${audienceClass}:${userId}`), or cache the raw ProfileRecord and run viewFor after the read so the filter is applied on every response. Bump the version segment so the v2 entries built under the old key are abandoned.

triage.reason: viewFor is the compensating control and the cache read at :56-61 returns before it runs. There is no other filter between loadProfile and the response.

The fields the cache leaks are email, phone, mfaEnrolled and recoveryCodesLeft (ProfileRecord, store.ts:25-33). Contact details and MFA state are personal data by any reading, and the code itself treats them as privileged by gating them at :39.
No narrowing condition exists: profileKey takes one argument, the subject id, and both call sites (:56 and :100) pass only that.

findings.title: The profile write check is satisfied by a scope every ordinary member holds, so any member can rewrite any other user's profile in any organisation
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: every member holds profile:write
findings.evidence: The check is `if (session.userId !== id && !hasScope(session.scopes, "profile:write"))` — deny only when the caller is not the subject AND lacks profile:write. The scope table at store.ts:44-49 grants member: ['profile:read', 'profile:write']. Scopes are derived from roles at mintSession (:69), so every member carries profile:write, the right-hand operand is false for them, and the conjunction never denies. The subject check on the left is therefore dead for the baseline role. Nothing else constrains it: there is no org comparison anywhere in the handler, unlike viewFor at :37 which does compare session.orgId to record.orgId. The write then lands at :99 under `directory:${id}`, which is the key loadProfile reads from (store.ts:143).
findings.impact: Any authenticated member rewrites the displayName and phone of any user in any organisation, cross-tenant, by id. The phone number is the interesting one: it is a recovery and MFA channel, so overwriting it is a step in an account-takeover chain rather than cosmetic vandalism. The write is also durable — the directory record is stored with a one-year TTL at :99 — while the victim's own view of it comes from the cache SB-04 describes.
findings.recommendation: Split the scope: keep profile:write for editing one's own record and introduce a distinct administrative scope for editing another's, granting the latter only to admin. Then make the check positive rather than a negated conjunction — establish that the caller is the subject, or holds the administrative scope and shares the subject's org — and add the org comparison the read path already performs at :37.

triage.reason: requireSession (main.ts:46) establishes that a caller is signed in and nothing more; it sets ctx.state.session and calls next (require_session.ts:33-34). No layer below re-checks ownership: writeCached at store.ts:138 takes the key it is given.
Not intended: the handler's own error message at :82 is 'not your profile', so the author intended the subject check to bind. The scope table is what silently defeats it.

FP-11 would apply if the scope were narrower than it reads. The opposite is true here — profile:write reads like a privileged grant and is held by the baseline role, so the construct applies to more than it appears to, not less.

findings.title: The remember-me branch writes the session cookie by hand, dropping the Secure and SameSite attributes the shared helper exists to guarantee, for the longest-lived cookie the service issues
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: remember-me cookie skips the helper
findings.evidence: session/cookie.ts:62-75 is the single place that is supposed to know how a session cookie is shaped, and its doc comment at :58-61 states the three properties it guarantees: unreachable from script, TLS only, never attached to a cross-site navigation — implemented as httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' at :68-70. The remember-me branch at auth.ts:35-39 calls ctx.cookies.set directly with only path, domain and maxAge. The comment at :32-34 gives the reason — the helper pins the lifetime to the session TTL and takes no argument for the longer window — but the helper does take that argument: ttlSeconds is its third parameter, defaulted at cookie.ts:65. So the entire divergence was unnecessary, and it applies to the thirty-day cookie (config.rememberTtlSeconds, config.ts:7) rather than the twelve-hour one. config.cookieDomain defaults to '.northwind.test' (config.ts:10), a leading-dot parent domain, so whatever attributes are lost are lost across every sibling host under it.
findings.impact: The month-long session cookie is sent on plaintext HTTP requests to any host under the parent domain, exposing it to a network observer, and is attached to cross-site requests, which reinstates CSRF against every state-changing route that authenticates by cookie — including PATCH /profile/:id. The wildcard domain widens both: any subdomain, including one that is not this service, can receive it.
findings.recommendation: Delete the hand-rolled branch and call `setSessionCookie(ctx, session.id, config.rememberTtlSeconds)` — the helper already accepts the lifetime. Then make the helper the only way to set that cookie name, so a future divergence has to be deliberate. Scope the cookie to the exact host rather than the parent domain unless sibling hosts genuinely need it.

triage.reason: The exculpation would be that oak v12.6.1's Cookies.set supplies safe defaults for the omitted attributes. I can establish that it cannot for two of them — secure defaults to false in any reading, since setting it true requires a secure request context, and sameSite has no cookie-spec default that would produce 'lax' — but for httpOnly the framework's own default is not determinable from this tree, which ships only the import URL at deps.ts:1 and no vendored source. So the finding is stated on Secure and SameSite and capped at probable. What would settle it: oak 12.6.1's cookies.ts, or a test asserting the Set-Cookie header this branch emits.
The branch is production login code reached whenever the request body carries remember: true (:31); it is not behind a development flag or a test double.
Not an absent defence beside a working equivalent — this is the only place these attributes are set for this cookie, and the helper that would set them is bypassed rather than duplicated.

findings.title: The identity-provider return endpoint redirects to any URL supplied in the query string
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: open redirect on /auth/continue
findings.evidence: `const next = ctx.request.url.searchParams.get("next") ?? "/dashboard";` at :60 followed by `ctx.response.redirect(next);` at :61. There is no scheme check, no host check, no leading-slash requirement and no allowlist — the default is relative but any absolute URL supplied by the caller is passed straight to the Location header. The route's comment at :57-58 describes the intent: the identity provider bounces the browser here with whatever the caller was part way through, which is precisely the flow that makes an open redirect valuable, because the victim expects a redirect at this point and the link legitimately originates on the accounts host.
findings.impact: A link to https://accounts.northwind.test/auth/continue?next=https://attacker.example carries the real, trusted hostname through mail filters and past a user checking the domain, and lands them on an attacker page — typically a replica of the sign-in form they were just using. It also launders the trusted origin into anything that allowlists redirect targets by their initial host, and can be used to forward a token or code appended to the target.
findings.recommendation: Accept only a path: reject any next that does not begin with a single '/' followed by a non-slash character, which excludes both absolute URLs and protocol-relative '//host' forms. If cross-host returns are genuinely needed, compare the parsed target's host against config.allowedHosts — the list already exists at config.ts:11 — and fall back to /dashboard on any mismatch.

triage.reason: The host allowlist at main.ts:18-28 is the only candidate and it constrains the inbound Host header of the request, not the outbound Location header. Nothing inspects the value between :60 and :61.
The value is read directly from the query string with no allowlist; only the absent case is defaulted.
The redirect is as wide as it reads. It is not narrowed to relative paths by a check elsewhere in the handler, which is two lines long and quoted in full above.

findings.title: With no signing keys configured, signing silently uses the literal string "undefined" as the key and verification rejects every cookie, downgrading the whole service to the unsigned legacy path
findings.class: insecure failure mode on missing configuration
findings.unaided_label: session-broker: empty signing key list degrades silently
findings.evidence: signingKeys (config.ts:22-27) reads SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS, splits on commas and filters empties, so an unset variable yields []. sign then destructures `const [current] = signingKeys()` at :31, giving undefined, and passes it to hmacHex, where `encoder.encode(key)` encodes undefined as the nine-byte string 'undefined' — a valid, non-empty, entirely public key. Nothing between config.ts:22 and cookie.ts:32 tests whether the list is empty. verify, meanwhile, iterates the same empty array at :43-46 and reaches `return null` at :46 for every input, so no cookie this service ever issued verifies, and require_session.ts:21 falls through to decodeLegacy for all of them. The application starts, logs in, and serves traffic throughout.
findings.impact: In the misconfigured state — a missing environment variable, a rotation that clears the list, a secrets mount that fails — every cookie is signed with a key an attacker can guess in one try, and simultaneously every cookie is accepted through the unsigned legacy path of SB-02. The service reports no error at any point, so the condition is invisible until someone reads the code. Even in the correctly configured state, the missing empty-list check is what allows a rotation mistake to become an authentication bypass rather than an outage.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed at startup: assert that signingKeys() is non-empty before the listener is opened at main.ts:56, and throw from sign if there is no current key rather than encoding undefined. Verification should already reject when the list is empty; make that state loud rather than silent by refusing to start.

triage.reason: No startup validation exists anywhere: main.ts:55-57 calls buildApp().listen with no configuration assertions, and config.ts performs no checks beyond trimming and filtering.

The exculpation would be a deployment manifest that guarantees SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS is always set. No manifest, compose file, chart or environment definition ships in this tree — the only reference to the variable is the read at config.ts:23. Per FP-08's doctrine, absence of evidence is not HOLDS, so this caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the deployment definition for this service.
The resulting key is the literal 'undefined', a value any attacker can reproduce without controlling anything — which is the exculpation this rule usually grants and here is exactly the defect.

findings.title: The firmware group is registered off the engine root rather than under the authenticated group, so anyone can upload an arbitrary image into any channel
findings.class: missing authentication on a code-distribution endpoint
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: firmware group is outside the auth group
findings.evidence: Line 30 builds the authenticated group as `api := r.Group("/v1", middleware.RequireFleetToken(deps.Store))`. Line 43 builds `fw := r.Group("/v1/firmware")` from `r`, the engine, not from `api`. Gin composes middleware by the receiver a group is created from, not by URL prefix, so fw inherits only the engine-level chain registered at :15-16 — Recovery, RequestLog, CanonicalPath and PerClientRate — and never RequireFleetToken. Both firmware routes hang off it: GET at :44 and, decisively, PUT at :45. handlers/firmware.go:37-62 then takes both path parameters straight from the request, creates the channel directory (:39), opens the destination with O_CREATE|O_TRUNC (:45) and copies up to 512 MiB of request body into it (:52). Nothing in the handler checks a signature, an extension, a magic number or a caller.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller writes a file of their choosing, under a name and channel of their choosing, into the firmware root — the directory the comment at :35-36 says release engineering promotes builds into and the provisioning rsync job picks up. Because the image is never signature-checked before or after the write, this is arbitrary firmware distribution to the fleet. It chains directly with FR-02 and FR-04: the same unauthenticated attacker repins any device to the channel they just wrote. O_TRUNC also means an existing legitimate image can be overwritten in place, and the same group's unauthenticated GET lets the attacker read every image back for offline analysis.
findings.recommendation: Create the firmware group from the authenticated group — `fw := api.Group("/firmware")` — so it cannot be reached without a token, and require an elevated role on PUT specifically, as EnqueueCommand already does for its admin-only commands. Independently of authentication, verify a detached signature over the image against a pinned release key before the bytes are committed to the channel directory, and have the devices verify it again at flash time.

triage.reason: The four engine-level middlewares are named above and none authenticates: CanonicalPath rejects dot segments (middleware/auth.go:57), PerClientRate shapes request rate, RequestLog writes a line, Recovery catches panics. RequireFleetToken is bound to the api group only, at router.go:30.

The comment at :40-42 claims the gateways pull over the provisioning VLAN, which if true would bound the read. It does not bound the write in any case, and there is no network policy, listener restriction or interface binding in the tree to substantiate it — main.go:46 binds cfg.Listen, defaulting to ':8080' on all interfaces (config/config.go:26).

A second principal is named even under the most generous reading of the comment at :40-42. If the route were reachable only from the provisioning VLAN, every gateway on that VLAN is still a distinct principal that can write an image the whole fleet then flashes — and the relay's own model treats devices as untrusted, since it authenticates them by token elsewhere (middleware/auth.go:31-45). The assertion reported here is that the group carries no authentication and the handler verifies no signature, neither of which a network boundary supplies.

findings.title: The authentication skip matches any path containing "/health", which includes the device heartbeat route, leaving it unauthenticated
findings.class: authentication bypass through an over-broad substring match
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: skipsAuth matches health-report
findings.evidence: `return strings.Contains(path, "/health") || path == "/metrics"`. The second operand is an exact comparison; the first is an unanchored substring test. Router line 35 registers `api.POST("/devices/:id/health-report", deps.HealthReport)` — a path that contains '/health'. RequireFleetToken consults skipsAuth first at :26 and calls c.Next() at :27, returning before the token is read at :31, so the handler runs with neither CtxTenantID nor CtxRole ever set. The comment at :17-19 explains the intent as liveness probes and heartbeats, but '/health' as a substring reaches far past a probe: any current or future route whose path contains that sequence anywhere is exempt.
findings.impact: POST /v1/devices/<id>/health-report is reachable with no credential, and FR-04 shows what that handler does with an unauthenticated request: it writes a heartbeat and sets the device's firmware channel by id alone. The tenant string the handler passes downstream is empty because nothing populated the context. Combined with FR-01, an attacker with no token uploads an image and then repins arbitrary devices to it.
findings.recommendation: Replace the substring test with an exact allowlist of the paths that genuinely need no token — '/v1/public/status' and '/metrics' — matched with ==, and move liveness onto a path that cannot collide with a resource route. The heartbeat is a device action with a device credential available; authenticate it rather than exempting it, and if the token lookup load is the real concern, cache the lookup rather than skipping it.

triage.reason: No layer below re-establishes the caller. HealthReport reads c.Param("id") and the request body directly (handlers/devices.go:110, :116), and the store methods it calls take no tenant argument at all (store/devices.go:126, :136).
The matched value is c.Request.URL.Path, taken from the request line. The route that collides is a registered application route, not a hypothetical.
This is FP-11 inverted. The construct reads as an exemption for health probes and applies to strictly more than that — the substring form is wider than the name suggests, not narrower.

findings.title: A bearer token with no row in token_roles is accepted and granted the baseline operator role, so any string authenticates
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: unknown token resolves to operator
findings.evidence: RoleForToken hashes the presented token and looks up token_roles by digest (:49-53). On sql.ErrNoRows it returns `Principal{Role: baselineRole}, nil` at :59, where baselineRole is the constant "operator" (:46) — a successful result, not an error. The middleware's rejection at middleware/auth.go:42 fires only when principal.Role is the empty string, and "operator" is not empty, so the request proceeds and c.Set stores an empty TenantID and the operator role (:47-48). The only inputs an attacker needs are a non-empty Authorization header, since the empty-token branch at :32 is the sole other rejection. The comment at :42-45 states the intent — pre-rollout gateways with no role row — but the fallback is keyed on the absence of a row, which is indistinguishable from an unknown token, so it applies to every token that was never issued rather than to a known set of legacy devices.
findings.impact: Authentication is decorative: `Authorization: Bearer x` reaches every route in the api group as an operator. That is ListDevices, RegisterDevice, GetDevice, HealthReport, EnqueueCommand and RetryFailed. The tenant is empty, which bounds the tenant-filtered reads to nothing, but three of those handlers do not filter by tenant at all — FR-04 and FR-05 — so the empty tenant is no protection where it matters. adminOnlyCommands still blocks collect-logs (handlers/commands.go:44), which is the only limit this role carries.
findings.recommendation: Return an error, or a Principal with an empty role, on sql.ErrNoRows so the middleware's existing rejection at auth.go:42-45 fires. If genuinely un-migrated gateways must keep working, enumerate them: add the legacy tokens to token_roles with an explicit restricted role and a dated expiry, so the exception is a list someone can audit rather than a default someone can guess into.

triage.reason: The middleware is the compensating layer and it is quoted: it rejects only Role == "" (auth.go:42), which this path never returns. No handler re-validates the principal.

The exposure is neither intended in this form nor bounded. The comment describes a bounded population — gateways provisioned before the role column existed — but nothing in the code restricts the fallback to them; it triggers on any digest miss.

The empty TenantID is the candidate narrowing, and it fails: SetFirmwareChannel (store/devices.go:136), RecordHeartbeat (:126) and the device_id path of EnqueueCommand (:186) carry no tenant predicate, so an empty tenant does not confine them.

findings.title: The heartbeat handler sets a device's firmware channel by id with no tenant, ownership or value check, and the serial it appears to require is never enforced
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: firmware channel set with no tenant or ownership check
findings.evidence: `update devices set firmware_channel = $2, channel_changed_at = now() where id = $1` — the predicate is the device id alone. No tenant_id, no serial. Its caller, handlers/devices.go:116, passes c.Param("id") and rep.FirmwareChannel, both from the request, and never consults middleware.CtxTenantID even though the sibling handlers on either side do (ListDevices at :65, GetDevice at :83). RecordHeartbeat, called two lines earlier at :110, does carry a serial predicate (`where id = $1 and serial = $2`, store:130) — but ExecContext returns no error when zero rows match, so a wrong serial produces no failure and execution falls straight through to the channel update at :115-120. The serial therefore reads as an ownership check and enforces nothing. The channel value itself is an arbitrary string: there is no allowlist, and it flows into the filesystem path at handlers/firmware.go:16 when a device fetches its image.
findings.impact: Any caller who knows a device id repins that device to any channel, cross-tenant. Via FR-02 that caller needs no token at all, and via FR-01 they can first create the channel and put an image in it. The device then pulls and flashes what the attacker wrote — this is the last link that turns two authentication defects into fleet-wide code execution. Device ids are UUIDs, but GetDevice and ListDevices hand them out to any principal, which FR-03 makes anyone.
findings.recommendation: Add `and tenant_id = $3` to both statements and pass the authenticated tenant, then check the affected row count and return an error when it is zero, so a mismatched serial or foreign device fails loudly instead of silently. Constrain firmware_channel to a server-side allowlist before it is written. A device should not be able to nominate its own channel in the first place — invert the flow so the relay tells the gateway which channel it is on.

triage.reason: The serial predicate on the neighbouring statement is the apparent compensating control and it is inert for the reason given: ExecContext does not error on zero rows affected, and handlers/devices.go:110-113 branches only on err.

Both the id and the channel come from the request — c.Param("id") and the bound JSON field rep.FirmwareChannel (handlers/devices.go:96, :116). The binding tag at :96 supplies no validation for that field.

A second principal is explicit: devices carry a tenant_id column (store:117) and every other read in the file filters on it, so the tenant boundary exists and this pair of statements is where it is not crossed but simply absent.

findings.title: Command enqueue takes the target device id from the request body and never binds it to the caller's tenant, and the response returns the foreign device's serial
findings.class: authorization checked on the caller, not on the object named in the body
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: command device_id never bound to the tenant
findings.evidence: The handler validates the command name against an allowlist (:38) and the role for admin-only commands (:44), then calls d.Store.EnqueueCommand with the authenticated tenant and req.DeviceID — a bare JSON field (:26) — side by side, with no query establishing that the device belongs to that tenant. The store writes the row as given (:184-187) and its RETURNING clause is `id, (select serial from devices where id = $2)` (store:186): a subquery on the device id with no tenant predicate. The handler then serialises command_id, device_serial and dispatch_token into the response (:67-71). So the tenant is used to label the row and never to authorise the target.
findings.impact: An authenticated principal of one tenant queues reboot, resync-config or set-beacon-interval against any device in any other tenant by id — remote disruption of another customer's fleet, with reboot on the allowlist. The response leaks the victim device's serial number, confirming the id is real and turning a blind guess into an oracle, and it hands back a dispatch_token minted for a device the caller does not own. Combined with FR-03, the caller needs no valid token to do it.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the device through a tenant-scoped lookup before enqueueing — the pattern already exists at store/devices.go:79 — and return 404 when it does not resolve. Add `and tenant_id = $1` to the RETURNING subquery so it cannot read across the boundary even if the handler check is later removed. This is the class where the route authorises the caller and nothing authorises the row the body names.

triage.reason: The two checks in the handler are quoted and neither concerns the device: allowedCommands tests the command name (:38), adminOnlyCommands tests the role (:44). The insert at store:184 has no scoping subquery in its WHERE and the table has no row-level policy anywhere in the tree.
req.DeviceID is bound from the JSON body at commands.go:26 with `binding:"required"` only, which asserts presence and nothing else.

The values crossing the boundary are a device serial and a dispatch_token — an identifier used to authorise the command against the gateway, per its name and its role in the response — not public or synthetic data.

findings.title: The idempotency cache is a process-global map keyed on the client's header alone, with no tenant in the key and no eviction
findings.class: cross-tenant disclosure through a shared cache key
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: idempotency cache is global and never evicted
findings.evidence: s.idem is a single map[string]json.RawMessage on the Store (:21), and both accessors key it on the raw Idempotency-Key header with nothing else: Idempotent reads s.idem[key] (:241), RememberIdempotent writes s.idem[key] (:248). The handler takes that header directly — `key := c.GetHeader("Idempotency-Key")` at commands.go:49 — and on a hit returns the stored bytes verbatim at :52, before the command name allowlist, before the role check and before any tenant is consulted. What is stored is the full response body from :67-71: command_id, device_serial and dispatch_token. There is no TTL, no size cap and no eviction anywhere; the map only grows.
findings.impact: Two effects. A caller who presents a key another tenant used receives that tenant's cached response, including the device serial and the dispatch_token minted for their command — and because the replay at :52 precedes every check in the handler, it is returned even for a command the caller's role could not issue. Separately, the map is an unbounded allocation driven by an attacker-chosen header value, so a stream of distinct keys grows the process heap without limit until the relay is killed; via FR-03 that requires no valid credential.
findings.recommendation: Key the entry on the tenant as well as the header value, and treat a key presented by a different tenant as a miss rather than a hit. Move the replay check after the authorization checks so a cached body cannot bypass them. Replace the map with a bounded, expiring cache — an LRU with a TTL matched to the retry window — or persist the keys in Postgres with the tenant as part of the primary key, which also survives a restart.

triage.reason: The replay path returns at commands.go:52 before any check runs; nothing between GetHeader at :49 and c.Data at :52 consults the principal. Store methods take no tenant argument for this map.
Both the key and the number of distinct keys are attacker-controlled: the value is an arbitrary request header, unvalidated and unbounded in length or count.
The cached body contains dispatch_token, which by its name and its use in the command flow is a per-command authorisation value, plus a device serial belonging to another tenant.

findings.title: Outbound TLS certificate verification is disabled by a default that is only correct when FLEET_ENV is explicitly set to "prod"
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: InsecureSkipVerify on by default
findings.evidence: `AllowInsecureTLS: env != "prod"` at :30, where env comes from `getenv("FLEET_ENV", "staging")` at :22 — so the value is true unless the variable is set, and set to exactly that one string. It flows straight into main.go:37 as `TLSClientConfig: &tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: cfg.AllowInsecureTLS}` on the callbacks client, which main.go:32-33 describes as the outbound leg the relay uses to call back into each site's device gateway and confirm a command landed. The comparison is exact and case-sensitive: "production", "Prod" and an unset variable all yield insecure. The comment at :28-29 gives the reason — lab and regional gateways terminating on an internal CA that is not in the runtime image — which is a certificate-distribution problem being solved by disabling verification globally.
findings.impact: Every callback the relay makes to a site gateway accepts any certificate, so anyone positioned on that path impersonates the gateway, reads the command confirmations and returns forged ones. The failure is silent and fails open on absence: a deployment that forgets the variable, spells it differently, or loses it in a config refactor is insecure with no error, and there is no startup log of the resulting value. The same env value gates nothing else, so nothing else in the deployment would look wrong.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default so the insecure path requires opting in — a distinct FLEET_ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS variable that must be set true explicitly, never derived from the environment name — and refuse it when FLEET_ENV is prod. Then remove the need for it: load the internal CA bundle into the client's RootCAs so lab and regional gateways verify properly rather than not at all.

triage.reason: There is no compensating layer for a client that skips verification: the flag is read once at main.go:37 into the Transport used for every callback, and no per-request check re-validates the peer.

The path ships. It is selected by an environment variable read at runtime (config.go:22), not by a build tag, a debug assertion or a test-only file, and the insecure value is what an unset variable produces.

A deployment manifest that reliably sets FLEET_ENV=prod would bound this in production, and no manifest, chart or compose file ships in the tree — the only reference to the variable is the read at config.go:22. Per FP-08 the absence of that artifact is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, and it caps this finding at probable. What would settle it: the deployment definition for this service, or a startup assertion in the code.

findings.title: The rate limiter's bucket map is keyed on a client-supplied address and is never swept, so it grows without bound
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: rate limit buckets never swept, key from ClientIP
findings.evidence: buckets is a package-level map[string]*bucket (:22) into which PerClientRate inserts a new entry for every previously unseen key (:35-39) and never deletes one — grep for delete(buckets across the tree returns nothing. The struct carries a `seen time.Time` field (:17) that is assigned on every request at :40 and read nowhere: grep for `seen` across fleet-relay returns the declaration, that one assignment, and unrelated last_seen columns in the store. A field whose only purpose is to drive an eviction sweep, with the sweep never written, is the declared-limit-with-no-enforcer shape. The key is `c.ClientIP()` (:32), which in gin resolves from the X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP headers when the peer is a trusted proxy, and gin.New() leaves the trusted-proxy set at its permissive default rather than narrowing it — router.go:14 configures no SetTrustedProxies call anywhere.
findings.impact: Two effects from one construct. Memory: each distinct key permanently costs a map entry and a rate.Limiter, so a stream of requests with varying source keys grows the process heap until the relay is OOM-killed, taking the fleet's command path with it — and via FR-03 the requests need no valid credential, while via FR-02 the health-report route needs no token at all. Evasion: if the deployment sits behind any proxy, the key is a header the caller writes, so rotating it defeats the limiter completely and the protection the comment at :25-27 describes — keeping one misbehaving gateway from starving the rest — does not hold.
findings.recommendation: Add the sweep the seen field was written for: a background ticker that walks the map under the mutex and deletes buckets untouched for longer than a few limiter windows, or replace the map with a bounded LRU. Separately, call SetTrustedProxies with the actual proxy CIDRs on the engine at router.go:14 so ClientIP resolves from a header only where a header is trustworthy, and key the limiter on the authenticated tenant as well as the address so an unauthenticated flood cannot displace legitimate buckets.

triage.reason: No layer bounds the map. gin's own middleware chain at router.go:15-16 adds no cache or eviction, and rate.Limiter itself holds no expiry — it is a token bucket with no lifecycle.

Even setting the header question aside, the number of distinct source addresses is attacker-controlled in the ordinary case of a distributed client set, and each one costs a permanent allocation. The unbounded-growth half of this finding does not depend on the X-Forwarded-For behaviour.

The benign reading of the reported defect would be that rate.Limiter or the map expires entries on its own, making the absent sweep harmless. Neither does: golang.org/x/time/rate holds a token bucket with no lifecycle, and a Go map releases nothing until a key is deleted. The `seen` field written at :40 and read nowhere is the author's own record that a sweep was intended. (The separate evasion effect described in the impact depends on gin's trusted-proxy resolution, which cannot be pinned without a go.mod; it is stated there as conditional and the finding does not rest on it.)

findings.title: The access log interpolates the decoded request path, so a caller can write newlines into it and forge log records
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: request path logged unescaped
findings.from_tool: not produced by log_escaper.py — that tool returned UNMEASURED (exit 2, no Python in the tree). Found by the hand enumeration of 11 log sinks that replaced it.
findings.evidence: `log.Printf("%s %s %d %s", c.Request.Method, c.Request.URL.Path, c.Writer.Status(), time.Since(start))`. The second verb takes URL.Path, which in Go's net/url is the percent-decoded form of the path — ParseRequestURI unescapes it, so a request target containing %0D%0A arrives at this line as a literal carriage return and newline. log.Printf writes to the standard logger, which emits one line-oriented record per call with a timestamp prefix, so anything after the injected newline reads as a record of its own. Nothing neutralises the value on the path: RequestLog is registered globally at router.go:15 alongside CanonicalPath, and CanonicalPath rejects only '..' (middleware/auth.go:57), not control characters. The middleware also runs for unmatched paths, since gin composes its global chain into the no-route handler, so the attacker is not restricted to the 42 registered routes and does not need to reach a handler at all.
findings.impact: One request produces two or more log records, with the forged one under the attacker's control — a fabricated 200 for an endpoint that was never called, an entry attributed to another address, or noise sized to bury a real event. That destroys the log's value as an incident record precisely when it is needed, and any consumer that parses line by line, alerts on a prefix, or renders the line into a page inherits the injection. Per WEB-28 the highest-yield case is exactly this one: a value an unauthenticated caller controls, and via FR-02 and FR-03 this relay has no meaningful authentication boundary in front of it anyway.
findings.recommendation: Log the value through a structured encoder that escapes control characters — a JSON handler in log/slog, with the path as a field rather than a format argument — and make sure the consumer parses that format. If line-oriented text must be kept, strip or percent-re-encode CR, LF and other C0 controls before the value reaches the format string, and use RawPath in preference to Path where it is set.

triage.reason: The value is the request path, chosen entirely by the caller, with no allowlist or pattern applied before the call. The only filter on the path is the '..' rejection at auth.go:57.

The sink re-parses in the relevant sense: log.Printf emits line-oriented text through the standard logger, and a newline in the argument therefore terminates the record. This is the distinction WEB-28 calls the whole triage, and it is the opposite of session-broker/main.ts:36, where the WHATWG pathname stays percent-encoded and the same construct is ruled out.
The benign reading would be that Go leaves the path encoded. It does not: URL.Path is documented as the decoded form and RawPath exists precisely to retain the original when the two differ.

This is not an absent defence beside a working one. The forged record is the impact, and no other mechanism in the tree preserves log integrity. Severity is held at medium because reaching code execution requires a rendering consumer this tree does not show.

findings.title: The retry sweep re-queues timed-out commands without the role check the enqueue path applies, so an operator can re-issue admin-only commands
findings.class: a gate one sibling handler enforces and another does not
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: retry re-queues admin-only commands
findings.evidence: EnqueueCommand gates the elevated command explicitly: `if adminOnlyCommands[req.Name] && role != "fleet-admin"` returns 403 at :44-47, with adminOnlyCommands = {"collect-logs": true} at :23 and the comment at :21-22 explaining that collect-logs ships the device's rolling buffer back and therefore needs the elevated role. RetryFailed, in the same file, reads only the tenant (:85), fetches every timed-out command in the window (:87) and pushes each back on the queue through EnqueueRaw (:95). It never reads middleware.CtxRole — grep for CtxRole in the package returns commands.go:43 and nothing else — and FailedCommands selects by tenant and state alone (store:212-216), returning rows of any name including collect-logs. EnqueueRaw re-inserts the row as stored (store:202-205). The comment at :80-82 states the justification — the rows already went through EnqueueCommand — which is true of how they were created and says nothing about who is replaying them.
findings.impact: An operator without fleet-admin calls POST /v1/commands/retry and re-queues every timed-out collect-logs command in their tenant, causing devices to ship their rolling log buffers — the support data the role gate exists to restrict. The effect is bounded to the caller's own tenant and to commands that already exist and timed out, which is why this is medium rather than high, but it is a real bypass of a check the codebase deliberately wrote two functions earlier.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same predicate on the retry path: skip, or refuse the whole sweep, when the caller lacks fleet-admin and the batch contains an admin-only command. Better, lift the decision out of both handlers into one function that takes the command name and the role, and call it from EnqueueCommand and from the retry loop, so a third caller cannot be added without it.

triage.reason: RequireFleetToken establishes a role and stores it (middleware/auth.go:48); it does not compare it to anything. The store layer has no authorization: EnqueueRaw inserts what it is handed (store:202).
No out-of-repository control is in question here — both handlers are in the same file and the check is present in one and absent in the other.

The benign reading would be that the two handlers do not reach the same effect. They do: both end in an insert into commands with state 'queued' (store:184-187 and :202-205), which is the same effect on the same table by the same mechanism.

findings.title: The default database connection string disables TLS
findings.class: insecure default for data in transit
findings.unaided_label: fleet-relay: sslmode=disable in the default DSN
findings.evidence: `DatabaseURL: getenv("FLEET_DATABASE_URL", "postgres://fleet@localhost:5432/fleet?sslmode=disable")`. getenv falls back whenever the variable is unset or empty (:37-41), and the comment at :19-20 states the intent plainly: anything not set falls back to what the docker-compose stack uses so a fresh checkout runs with no setup. The value is passed to sql.Open at store/devices.go:25 with no post-validation, and nothing anywhere asserts that the effective DSN requires TLS. Enumerated key by key, this file also carries FR-07's AllowInsecureTLS at :30; the remaining five keys — FLEET_LISTEN, FLEET_COMMAND_TTL, FLEET_FIRMWARE_ROOT, FLEET_RATE_BURST and FLEET_ENV itself — are unobjectionable in isolation.
findings.impact: If the variable is ever unset in a real deployment, every statement, credential and row moves between the relay and Postgres in clear text, including the token_roles digests that are the whole authentication basis and the dispatch tokens in the commands table. Severity is low because the failure requires the variable to be missing and because the same fallback names localhost, which limits the blast radius to a host-local misconfiguration in most deployments.
findings.recommendation: Make FLEET_DATABASE_URL required — fail at startup rather than falling back — or at minimum default to sslmode=require. Keep the convenient developer default in a compose file or a .env.example rather than in the binary, so the ergonomics do not ride into production inside the code.

triage.reason: The fallback is in the shipped Load function, selected at runtime on the absence of an environment variable, not behind a build tag or a development-only file.

The exculpation would be that this link never crosses a trust boundary because the default names localhost. That holds only if the deployment actually runs Postgres on the same host, and no deployment artifact ships in the tree to establish it. Per FP-08's doctrine this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, which is consistent with the finding being reported at low rather than confirmed-high.
Transport encryption to the database is not defence in depth behind an equivalent control; nothing else in the tree protects that link.

findings.title: The label download joins an unvalidated tail path parameter onto the label root, and the sanitiser in the same handler is applied to the download name instead of the path
findings.unaided_label: parcel-track: label_ref tail joined onto label_root
findings.evidence: The route is `#[get("/labels/{shipment_id}/{label_ref:.*}")]` (:22) — the `:.*` tail form, which unlike a normal actix segment matches slashes, so label_ref can be a multi-segment path. The handler reads it at :28 and at :39 does `state.cfg.label_root.join(&label_ref)` followed by `fs::read(&file)` at :40, with no canonicalisation, no prefix assertion and no rejection of dot segments in between. PathBuf::join with a relative path containing '..' walks up out of the base. The file does contain a sanitiser — download_name at :13-20, which maps every character outside [A-Za-z0-9-_] to '_' — but it is applied at :46 to the Content-Disposition filename, not to the value used at :39. The ownership check above it (:30-37) verifies the caller owns shipment_id; it says nothing about label_ref. No NormalizePath middleware is registered in main.rs, and actix-files' traversal guard does not apply because this is a raw fs::read rather than a NamedFile.
findings.impact: An authenticated account holder — and any caller can become one, since accounts create their own shipments — requests GET /api/v1/labels/<a shipment they own>/../../../../etc/passwd and receives the file, served with a 200 and a laundered .pdf filename. Anything the service process can read is readable: application configuration and the DATABASE_URL in it, the accounts table's callback secrets if they are ever written to disk, container secrets under /var/run/secrets, and other accounts' label PDFs under the same root by direct name. The sanitiser sitting three lines below the vulnerable join is what makes this survive review — the file looks like it handles hostile names.
findings.recommendation: Do not accept a path from the client. Store labels under a server-generated name keyed to the shipment and look that name up from the database, so label_ref is an opaque identifier rather than a path. If the reference must stay caller-supplied, reject any value containing a separator or a dot segment before the join, then canonicalise with std::fs::canonicalize and assert the result still starts with label_root before opening — order matters, the assertion has to precede the read.

triage.reason: The two candidate controls both fail to cover the value. The ownership check at :30-37 constrains shipment_id only. download_name is applied at :46, after the read at :40, and to a different expression — a sanitiser on the wrong value is the canonical way FP-01 is answered wrongly, and it is answered here by quoting both line numbers.
label_ref is a route parameter extracted at :28 from a tail pattern that deliberately admits slashes. Nothing narrows it between extraction and the join.

The sink is fs::read on the composed path (:40) and the bytes are returned in the response body (:48). It reads and discloses whatever the resolved path names; the application/pdf content type at :43 is a label on the response, not a constraint on the file.

findings.title: Bulk import writes each row's attachment to a path built from a caller-supplied filename, creating directories as needed
findings.unaided_label: parcel-track: attachment_name joined onto import_root
findings.evidence: stage_attachment does `let target = root.join(name);` at :75, then `fs::create_dir_all(parent)` at :78 and `fs::write(&target, bytes)` at :81. name is BulkRow::attachment_name, a plain Option<String> deserialised from the JSON body (:25) with no validation anywhere — the handler passes it through untouched at :65. Because the value arrives in a JSON body rather than a URL, there is no routing layer, percent-decoding or path normalisation between the wire and the join; whatever bytes the caller wrote are what PathBuf::join receives. The bytes written are attachment_body, also caller-supplied (:27). The only limit in the handler is the row count check at :39, which bounds how many files are written, not where. The comment at :24 describes the intended value as customs paperwork, i.e. a filename.
findings.impact: An authenticated account posts one manifest row with attachment_name set to a relative path escaping import_root and attachment_body set to arbitrary content, and the service writes that file with the process's privileges — creating any missing parent directories on the way. Depending on what the process can reach, that is overwriting the application's own configuration, planting a file in a directory another component executes or ingests, appending to an authorized_keys file, or clobbering the label store that PT-01 reads. Combined with PT-01 the attacker can write a file and then read anything back, which makes exploration of the filesystem trivial.
findings.recommendation: Generate the stored filename server-side — a UUID, or a hash of the content — and keep the caller's name only as a database column for display. If the caller's name must shape the path, strip it to a bare basename, reject anything that is not a single path component matching a strict pattern, and canonicalise the composed path and assert it is inside import_root before writing. Remove the create_dir_all: staging into an existing directory is safer than letting a request create the tree it wants.

triage.reason: There is no validator on this path at all. The AuthGuard establishes an account (auth.rs:82-86) and nothing else touches attachment_name — grep for it across parcel-track returns the struct field at imports.rs:25 and the two uses at :64-65.
The value is a free-form JSON string field. serde applies no constraint beyond the String type, and the handler applies none.
The sink is fs::write to a composed path (:81), preceded by create_dir_all (:78) — a write that creates its own destination is dangerous in exactly the form it is reached.

findings.title: Webhook subscriptions can be rewritten by any account, because the update handler omits the ownership check its create sibling performs
findings.class: a gate one sibling handler enforces and another does not
