findings.unaided_label: parcel-track: update_subscription checks nothing
findings.from_tool: neighbourhood flagged by writer_parity.py (UNCHECKED on parcel-track/src/auth.rs:23 and :57 writing `principal` against a checked sibling); the specific asymmetry was established by reading create_subscription and update_subscription side by side
findings.evidence: create_subscription opens with `if body.account_id != principal.account_id { return Forbidden }` at :26-28, then validates the URL and inserts scoped to that account (:32-36). update_subscription, twenty lines below in the same file and taking the same SubscriptionPayload, validates the URL at :52 and then calls `state.store.update_subscription(id, &body.callback_url, &body.events)` at :54-58. The subscription id comes from the path (:47) and is never resolved against the caller: the store's statement is `update webhook_subscriptions set callback_url = $2, events = $3 where id = $1` (store.rs:164-167) with no account_id in the predicate, and the handler never reads principal.account_id except to log it at :60. The id is an i64, so it enumerates by counting.
findings.impact: Any account holder rewrites any other account's webhook subscription to a URL they control, and every subsequent scan event for that account is delivered to the attacker instead — shipment references, states and the delivery metadata the subscriber was paying to receive. The victim simply stops receiving their callbacks, which reads as an outage rather than a breach. The attacker also chooses the event list, so they can widen what is sent. It is a quiet, persistent interception of another customer's data feed established by one PUT.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the subscription with the account in the predicate — `where id = $1 and account_id = $2` — and return 404 when no row is affected, so the handler cannot address a foreign row at all. Apply the same account check create_subscription performs at :26 before the update, and add a test asserting account A cannot modify account B's subscription id.

triage.reason: The AuthGuard resolves an api key to a Principal (auth.rs:82-86) and injects it; it performs no per-object authorization. The store method is quoted above and has no account predicate. No middleware between them re-checks.
No out-of-repository control is in question — both handlers are in the same file and the check is present in one and absent in the other.

The benign reading would be that the two handlers do not reach the same effect. They do: both set callback_url and events on a webhook_subscriptions row, one by insert and one by update, from the same payload type.

findings.title: The callback URL validator blocks a handful of literal addresses and names, and passes every other route to the internal network
findings.unaided_label: parcel-track: SSRF denylist has holes
findings.evidence: The function requires https (:37), then denies three name suffixes — localhost, .internal, .cluster.local (:45) — and, only when host_str parses as a literal IpAddr (:49), denies IPv4 private, loopback and link-local, and IPv6 loopback and unspecified (:50-53). Four concrete gaps follow from those exact predicates. A hostname that resolves to an internal address is not a literal IpAddr, so the whole ip branch is skipped and any attacker-controlled DNS name pointing at 10.x or the metadata service passes. IPv4 0.0.0.0 satisfies none of is_private, is_loopback or is_link_local, and on Linux connects to localhost. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal such as [::ffff:127.0.0.1] or [::ffff:169.254.169.254] returns false from Ipv6Addr::is_loopback and is_unspecified, so it passes and reaches the mapped destination. IPv6 unique-local fc00::/7 and link-local fe80::/10 are not tested at all. Validation also happens only at write time (:80, webhooks.rs:30 and :52); the request is made later from a different process state, so a name that resolved publicly at registration can resolve internally at delivery. The doc comment at :32-33 states the threat precisely — callbacks fire from inside the delivery VPC — which is what makes each gap consequential.
findings.impact: A subscriber registers a callback the service will then fetch from inside the delivery VPC, reaching services that have no authentication because they are not expected to be reachable: cloud metadata and its instance credentials, internal admin interfaces, databases, other tenants' services. Because PT-03 lets an attacker rewrite anyone's subscription, they need not even own the account whose callbacks carry the request.
findings.recommendation: Replace the denylist with an allowlist of subscriber domains where that is possible. Where it is not, resolve the hostname yourself, check every returned address against the reserved ranges — including IPv4-mapped, unique-local, link-local, CGNAT and unspecified — and connect to the address you validated rather than re-resolving, so the check cannot be undone between validation and connection. Disable redirect following, or re-validate each hop. Re-validate at delivery time, not only at registration.

triage.reason: No egress control ships in the tree: there is no proxy configuration, no network policy and no allowlist of destination hosts anywhere in parcel-track. This function is the only thing standing between the payload and the request.
callback_url is a caller-supplied field on both NewShipmentPayload (:18) and SubscriptionPayload (webhooks.rs:16). The scheme is constrained to https and nothing else is.

This rule would apply if the validator were narrower than it reads in a safe direction. It is the reverse: the predicates are exactly as written, and the concrete bypasses above are values they do not match rather than values a further condition catches.

findings.title: The unauthenticated tracking endpoint returns the full shipment record, including the recipient's name, street address and phone number
findings.class: excessive data exposure on an unauthenticated route
findings.unaided_label: parcel-track: status endpoint returns the whole recipient record
findings.evidence: auth.rs:23-25 exempts any path ending in /status from the guard, and the doc comment at :20-22 explains why: the recipient opens the tracking page from the carrier's SMS and holds no key. The handler at :129-139 takes no Principal, calls get_shipment_any_account (store.rs:105) — a query with no account predicate, as its name says — and serialises the result directly. That result is ShipmentView, whose fields are declared at :21-30: id, reference, state, recipient_name, recipient_address, recipient_phone and last_scan_at. It is the same struct the authenticated get_one returns at :101. So an endpoint deliberately built for an anonymous audience reuses the projection built for the account that owns the data, and no field filtering happens anywhere between the query and the response.
findings.impact: Anyone holding a tracking link — or who obtains one from a forwarded SMS, a shared screenshot, a browser history, a referrer header or a support ticket — gets the recipient's full name, delivery address and phone number, not merely the delivery state the page needs. That is a personal-data disclosure well beyond the intended function, and it makes any leak of a tracking URL a leak of a home address. The v4 UUID makes blind enumeration impractical, which bounds the severity, but it does nothing once a single link escapes.
findings.recommendation: Give the anonymous route its own projection carrying only state and last_scan_at, plus at most a masked reference — never the contact block. Keep ShipmentView for the authenticated handlers. This is the property-level half of the class: the route's authorization is intended, its serializer is what exceeds it.

triage.reason: There is no filtering layer between the store and the response. The handler returns HttpResponse::Ok().json(shipment) at :136 with the struct as fetched, and ShipmentView derives Serialize over all seven fields (:21-30).

The exposure is intended in part and the finding therefore moves rather than disappearing, exactly as FP-05 describes: what is intended is that a recipient sees delivery status without a key, and what is bounded by the UUID is discovery. Neither bounds the field set, which is the defect reported.
recipient_name, recipient_address and recipient_phone are personal data on any reading, and the application itself treats the same struct as account-scoped everywhere else it is returned.

findings.title: The carrier callback compares the HMAC with a non-constant-time string comparison and accepts a valid signature any number of times
findings.unaided_label: parcel-track: signature compared with !=, no replay window
findings.evidence: The handler computes the expected HMAC-SHA256 over the body correctly (:87-90) and then compares with `if provided != expected` at :92 — a plain &str inequality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and so takes a length of time correlated with the length of the matching prefix. The hmac crate exposes mac.verify_slice for exactly this reason and it is not used, even though the crate is already imported at :2. Separately, nothing in the request is bound to a point in time or to a single use: there is no timestamp header read, no nonce, no replay cache, and no check that a scan has not already been applied. apply_scans (store.rs:186-206) simply re-executes the updates. The route sits outside the guarded scope by design (main.rs:40-42), so the signature is the only authentication it has.
findings.impact: The timing side channel is the weaker half — it is a byte-at-a-time oracle over a network, which is slow and noisy but is the standard reason this comparison is called out. The replay half is directly practical: anyone who observes one signed callback can resend it unchanged, and the service will re-apply those scan states to the account's shipments. Since state is an arbitrary string (see the recommendation), replaying an older body reverts shipments to a stale state and can be repeated indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Compare with the constant-time verifier — `mac.verify_slice(&hex::decode(provided)?)` — rather than with !=. Require a timestamp header, include it in the signed material, reject anything outside a few minutes, and record recently seen signatures so a body cannot be applied twice. While in this handler, constrain the state value that apply_scans writes (store.rs:191 defaults it to in_transit and otherwise takes whatever string arrives) to a server-side allowlist.

triage.reason: The signature check is the only control on this route; main.rs:40-42 places it outside the AuthGuard scope deliberately, so there is no second layer and no replay protection elsewhere — grep for a timestamp or nonce across parcel-track returns nothing.
The comparison governs an access decision — the 401 at :93 — rather than feeding a log or a metric, and the accepted body is applied to the account's shipments at :99-103.

This is not defence in depth behind a working control; it is the control. Severity is set at low because remote timing extraction of an HMAC is expensive and the replay effect is bounded to re-applying scan states the carrier already sent, not because the impact fails to reach the user.

findings.title: The open-endpoint exemption is a suffix match, so it also exempts paths on the label route that were never meant to be public
findings.unaided_label: parcel-track: open-endpoint suffix is wider than the route
findings.from_tool: writer_parity.py flagged auth.rs:23 and auth.rs:57 as writing `principal` with no validator against a checked sibling
findings.evidence: `path.ends_with("/status") || path == "/healthz"`. The second operand is an exact match; the first is an unanchored suffix that the guard applies to the whole request path at :63 before any key is read. It is intended for exactly one route, /api/v1/shipments/{id}/status (shipments.rs:128). But labels::download is registered with a tail pattern, `#[get("/labels/{shipment_id}/{label_ref:.*}")]` (labels.rs:22), which matches any number of trailing segments — so a request to /api/v1/labels/<uuid>/anything/status matches that route and simultaneously satisfies the exemption, and the guard hands it straight to the handler at :64 with no Principal in the request extensions.
findings.impact: For the routes that exist today the practical effect is contained: labels::download declares `principal: web::ReqData<Principal>` (labels.rs:25), and that extractor fails when nothing inserted a Principal, so the request errors rather than reading a file unauthenticated. The finding is the construct rather than a demonstrated read — an exemption written for one endpoint that already reaches a second, on a route whose whole purpose is serving files, and that will silently cover any future path ending in /status or any handler that stops requiring ReqData.
findings.recommendation: Match the exemption exactly rather than by suffix: compare against a small list of complete paths, or move the public tracking endpoint under a dedicated prefix such as /public/ and exempt that prefix with a leading-boundary check. Tighten the label route's tail pattern to a single segment while doing so, since PT-01 shows the tail form is load-bearing in the wrong direction there too.

triage.reason: Whether the exemption is presently harmless depends on actix-web 4.5's behaviour when web::ReqData finds nothing in the extensions — it should produce an extractor error rather than a default Principal, but no lockfile ships and I did not execute the code, so I cannot establish it here. That caps this finding at probable and is why the impact is stated as contained rather than exploited. What would settle it: a request to /api/v1/labels/<uuid>/x/status against a running instance, or actix-web's ReqData::from_request implementation at the pinned version.
The exemption is intended for one endpoint and the comment at :20-22 names it. Reaching a second route is outside what is intended, so the exposure is not the bounded one the comment describes.

The construct is not narrower than it looks. The suffix test is applied to the full path at :63 with no prefix or route condition alongside it, and a registered tail route already widens it beyond the single endpoint it names.

findings.title: A legacy alias routes the adjustments controller to a path outside the /api/v1/admin prefix the role check keys on, so any partner can post money-moving corrections
findings.class: function-level authorization bypassed by an aliased route
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: legacy adjust route misses the admin prefix
findings.evidence: ApplicationController runs `before_action :require_admin, if: :admin_area?` at :8, and admin_area? is `request.path.start_with?(ADMIN_PATH_PREFIX)` at :29 with the prefix frozen as "/api/v1/admin" at :4. The canonical route reaches that prefix: `namespace :admin { resources :adjustments }` at routes.rb:22-24 produces /api/v1/admin/adjustments. The legacy alias at :30 maps to the same controller action — `post "invoices/:invoice_id/adjust", to: "admin/adjustments#create"` — but its path is /api/v1/invoices/:invoice_id/adjust, which does not start with the prefix, so admin_area? returns false and require_admin never runs. The routing comment at :26-29 states the aliases's purpose and asserts that nothing else had to change when the canonical route moved under /admin, which is exactly the assumption the guard's path-prefix design breaks. The controller itself carries no role check of its own — create at adjustments_controller.rb:20-34 goes straight from Invoice.find to Adjustment.create! to LedgerPosting#credit!.
findings.impact: Any authenticated partner posts an adjustment against an invoice, which the application controller's own comment at :26-27 identifies as the only place a partner can move money that has already been posted. The action creates the Adjustment row and then calls credit!, which writes a negative LedgerEntry and reduces the invoice amount. Combined with LA-02 the target invoice need not even belong to the caller's organisation, and with LA-08 the amount is not validated. This is unauthorised movement of posted financial records, reachable with an ordinary partner token.
findings.recommendation: Stop deriving authorization from the request path. Put `before_action :require_admin` in AdjustmentsController itself so every route that reaches the action is covered regardless of its URL, and keep the prefix rule only as a coarse second layer. Then add a test that enumerates every route mapping to an admin/* controller and asserts each returns 403 for a non-admin token — a check that would have caught this alias the day it was added.

triage.reason: The prefix guard at application_controller.rb:8 and :29 is the only function-level control, and its predicate is quoted above with the legacy path failing it. authenticate_partner! at :6 establishes identity only — it sets @current_user and returns a boolean about presence (:20-23). No policy object, no cancan ability, no Pundit call exists anywhere in the tree.
The route ships: it is declared unconditionally in config/routes.rb, not inside an environment guard or a feature flag, and the comment at :26-27 says the 2019 partner clients still use it.
The gap is not narrower than it reads. The alias maps to the same controller action as the guarded route, with the same payload shape by the comment's own account, so the effect reached is identical.

findings.title: Adjustment creation resolves the invoice with an unscoped finder, while its own index action scopes by organisation
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: adjustment create resolves the invoice unscoped
findings.evidence: index, fourteen lines above, joins and filters explicitly: `.where(invoices: { org_id: current_user.org_id })` at :8. create writes `invoice = Invoice.find(invoice_id)` at :21 — the bare model finder, with no org predicate. invoice_id is `params[:invoice_id].presence || adjustment_params[:invoice_id]` (:38-40), so the identifier comes from the URL or from the body, entirely caller-chosen. ApplicationController offers the correct helper — scoped_invoices at :46-48, `Invoice.where(org_id: current_user.org_id)` — and the sibling controller uses it at invoices_controller.rb:16 and :44. It is not used here. The resolved invoice is then passed to Adjustment.create! (:24-29) and to LedgerPosting.new(invoice).credit! (:31).
findings.impact: An adjustment can be posted against any invoice in the system by id, in any organisation. credit! writes a negative ledger entry and reduces that invoice's amount, so this is a direct, cross-tenant alteration of another customer's financial position — a write, not merely a read. Via LA-01 the caller does not need the admin role to reach it; via LA-08 the amount bypasses the model's validations. Invoice ids are sequential in a Rails schema, so targets enumerate.
findings.recommendation: Change line 21 to `scoped_invoices.find(invoice_id)`, which raises RecordNotFound for a foreign id and is already handled into a 404 by the rescue at application_controller.rb:10-12. Then grep the controllers for every bare Model.find and require the scoped helper by convention, with a request spec asserting an invoice in another org returns 404 on this action.

triage.reason: No mandatory scope exists below the controller. Invoice (app/models/invoice.rb) declares validations and callbacks but no default_scope and no multi-tenancy concern, and there is no row-level security or query interceptor anywhere in the tree.
invoice_id is read from params, taking the URL segment when present and the permitted body attribute otherwise (:38-40). Nothing constrains which invoice it may name.
The affected records are invoices and ledger entries belonging to another organisation — financial data with an owner, which the index action of this same controller treats as org-scoped.

findings.title: Invoice update uses the unscoped finder while index, show and void all use the organisation scope
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: invoice update resolves unscoped
findings.from_tool: line flagged by writer_parity.py (UNCHECKED against update() at ledger-api/app/controllers/api/v1/invoices_controller.rb:33); the scoped/unscoped asymmetry within the controller was established by reading
findings.evidence: Four actions in this controller resolve an invoice and three of them scope it: index at :7 (`scoped_invoices`), show at :16 (`scoped_invoices.find`), void at :44 (`scoped_invoices.find`). update at :34 is `Invoice.find(params[:id])`. The permitted attributes are not cosmetic: invoice_params at :52-54 admits reference, memo, amount_cents, currency, issued_on and posted_at, and the update at :36 applies all of them. The comment at :31-32 explains the intent as partners fixing typos in the reference and the memo line, but the permit list reaches the money column and the finder reaches every organisation.
findings.impact: Any authenticated partner rewrites any invoice in the system by id, cross-tenant: changing amount_cents alters what another organisation is owed, changing reference collides with or displaces their records, changing issued_on and posted_at moves a transaction between accounting periods. Unlike LA-02 this needs no admin route and no legacy alias — it is a plain PUT on the standard REST resource. The single-line divergence from its three siblings is what makes it invisible: the controller reads as consistently scoped.
findings.recommendation: Change line 34 to `scoped_invoices.find(params[:id])`, matching the three sibling actions. Narrow invoice_params for the update path to the fields the comment actually describes — reference and memo — so a scoping regression cannot again reach amount_cents, and reject changes to a posted or voided invoice outright.

triage.reason: No layer below re-scopes: the Invoice model has no default_scope, and the update at :36 is a plain ActiveRecord write. The three sibling actions demonstrate that scoping in this codebase is a controller-level convention with nothing enforcing it.
params[:id] is the URL segment, and no constraint is declared on it in config/routes.rb:9 — resources :invoices uses the default segment pattern.

A second principal is explicit and central: invoices carry org_id, scoped_invoices filters on it (application_controller.rb:47), and its comment at :45 states that every read and write goes through the caller's organisation — which this action does not.

findings.title: The export sort parameter is passed into Arel.sql, which is the documented way to bypass Rails' ORDER BY sanitisation
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: sort param into Arel.sql
findings.evidence: `column = params[:sort].presence || "issued_on"` at :16, then `.order(Arel.sql("#{column} #{direction}"))` at :19. Rails would normally reject a raw string in order with a disallowed-column error; Arel.sql exists precisely to tell it not to, so the framework's own protection is explicitly switched off around a caller-controlled value. The direction operand beside it shows the author knew the shape of the fix — `params[:dir] == "asc" ? "ASC" : "DESC"` at :15 is a correct two-value allowlist that never lets the parameter through — and the column was left unconstrained. There is no column allowlist anywhere in the file, and the comment at :12-13 states the value is passed through deliberately so finance can order the file the way their spreadsheet expects. ORDER BY is one of the positions that cannot be parameterised, so per WEB-07 an allowlist is the only valid control there and none exists.
findings.impact: The caller controls a raw SQL fragment in an ORDER BY on a query over the invoices table. In PostgreSQL that position accepts expressions and subselects, so it can be turned into a boolean or error oracle that reads any table the application role can reach — other organisations' invoices, the partners table and its client secrets, the api_tokens table — one predicate at a time, with the CSV response and the error path both usable as the channel. The endpoint requires only an ordinary partner token.
findings.recommendation: Map the parameter through a fixed allowlist to a literal column name, exactly as direction is handled two lines above: a hash from permitted sort keys to column names, falling back to issued_on for anything unrecognised, with Arel.sql applied to the resulting literal rather than to interpolated input. Then grep for every other Arel.sql in the codebase and confirm each one wraps a constant.

triage.reason: Rails' own ORDER BY sanitisation is the compensating control and Arel.sql is the documented opt-out from it, applied here directly to the interpolated string. No validation runs between :16 and :19 — the two lines are consecutive apart from the scoped_invoices call.
params[:sort] is read straight from the query string with only a presence check. coerce_pagination at application_controller.rb:40-43 normalises limit and offset and does not touch sort.
The construct is not narrower than it reads: the interpolation covers the whole column position, and the only neighbouring constraint applies to direction, not to column.

findings.title: Export listing and re-download operate on a shared directory with no organisation scoping, so a partner can enumerate and fetch every other partner's export
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: export list and stream ignore the org
findings.evidence: EXPORT_ROOT is a single directory for the whole application, `Rails.root.join("tmp", "exports")` at :6 — not per organisation. index returns `Dir.children(EXPORT_ROOT).sort` at :9, the raw filename list, with no filter of any kind. stream at :28-33 builds `EXPORT_ROOT.join("#{params[:path]}.csv")`, tests File.exist? and calls send_file — it never consults current_user or org_id, and it never looks the file up in a table that would record an owner. The controller has scoped_invoices available and uses it in create at :18, so the scoping helper is present in the same file and simply absent from these two actions. Note that path traversal here is separately ruled out by the route constraint at config/routes.rb:18; this finding needs no traversal, only the correct name, which index supplies.
findings.impact: Two ordinary requests compose into a full cross-tenant read: GET /api/v1/exports/list returns the filenames of every export on disk, and GET /api/v1/exports/stream/<name> returns that file. The files are ledger CSVs — reference, memo, amount_cents, currency, status and issued_on per HEADERS at :37 — so a partner obtains other partners' complete invoice histories. No guessing is required because the listing hands over the names.
findings.recommendation: Record exports as rows with an org_id and serve them by database id, resolving through the caller's organisation so a foreign id is a 404. Failing that, store them in per-organisation subdirectories derived server-side from current_user.org_id and never from a parameter, and filter index to the caller's directory. Give the files a TTL and a cleanup job as well — an unbounded directory of ledger extracts is a standing liability.

triage.reason: The route constraint at routes.rb:18 restricts the shape of the filename and says nothing about ownership, and it is the only control on the path. authenticate_partner! establishes identity only. No layer maps a file to an organisation anywhere in the tree.

Not an intended shared surface: the create action that produces exports is scoped to the caller's invoices at :18, so the data is org-private by the controller's own design and only the retrieval path forgets it.
The files are ledger extracts whose columns are enumerated at :37 — invoice references, memos and amounts belonging to a named organisation.

findings.title: The credential and token endpoints are the only unauthenticated routes in the API and the only ones no throttle covers
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: token endpoints unthrottled
findings.evidence: Three throttles are declared and each is bound to a path prefix: /api/v1/invoices at :18, /api/v1/exports at :22, /api/v1/admin at :26. Cross-referenced against config/routes.rb, the routes those prefixes do not cover are `post "tokens"` (:5), `post "tokens/refresh"` (:6) and `delete "tokens"` (:7). Those are precisely the routes TokensController exempts from authentication — `skip_before_action :authenticate_partner!, only: %i[create refresh]` at tokens_controller.rb:4 — so the two endpoints reachable with no credential are the two with no rate limit. create compares a client secret at :11 and refresh looks up a bearer refresh token at :20, both taken directly from params. The blocklist at :30-32 matches only three scanner user-agent strings and is trivially avoided by not sending them.
findings.impact: Unlimited unauthenticated attempts against partner client credentials and against refresh tokens, from a single address, with no lockout, no backoff and no counter. Credential stuffing and refresh-token guessing are both unbounded, and a successful hit yields a bearer token that reaches the whole API. The endpoint is also the cheapest denial-of-service target in the service, since each attempt runs a password-comparison.
findings.recommendation: Add a throttle for /api/v1/tokens with a limit far below the 300-per-five-minutes the invoice routes carry, and key it on the presented client_id as well as on the address so a distributed attempt against one partner is caught. Add an exponential backoff or lockout bound to the client_id rather than to the IP, and ensure a failed exchange logs an auditable event.

triage.reason: Rack::Attack is the only limiter in the tree — there is no DRF-style throttle, no per-controller limit and no middleware beyond this initializer — and its three rules are enumerated above with the token paths matching none of them.

An upstream WAF or API gateway could rate-limit this path, and no such configuration ships in the tree — there is no ingress definition, no nginx or Cloudflare config and no deployment manifest. Per FP-08 the absence of that artifact is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, and it caps this finding at probable. What would settle it: the edge configuration for this API. Note that even an address-keyed edge limiter would not supply the identity-keyed lockout the recommendation asks for, so part of this finding survives either answer.
The throttles are exactly as narrow as they read: each is a start_with? on one prefix, and no fourth rule or catch-all exists in the file.

findings.title: The bulk import takes each row's organisation from the uploaded file and writes through insert_all, which runs no model validation
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: import takes org_id from the row and skips validation
findings.evidence: build_row sets `org_id: row["org_id"].presence || upload.org_id` at :31 — the uploading organisation is only the fallback, and a value present in the CSV column wins. The rows are then written with `Invoice.insert_all(rows, returning: false)` at :19, which goes straight to SQL and runs no validations and no callbacks. app/models/invoice.rb declares exactly the invariants that bypasses: reference presence and per-org uniqueness (:8), amount_cents integer and greater than zero (:9), currency inclusion in a four-value list (:10), status inclusion in STATUSES (:11), issuer_belongs_to_org (:12), and the before_save assert_ledger_balanced (:15). build_row's own defaults show the fields are unconstrained on this path: amount_cents is `row["amount_cents"].to_i` (:34), which yields 0 for junk and accepts a negative, and status is whatever string the file carries (:36). The class comment at :3-4 states that the partner drops the CSV on the upload endpoint.
findings.impact: A partner who controls the uploaded file writes invoices directly into any other organisation by putting that org_id in a column, and writes them with values the model forbids: zero or negative amounts, an unlisted currency, an arbitrary status string including 'paid', and references that collide with existing ones because the uniqueness check never runs. That is both a cross-tenant write and a corruption of the ledger's stated invariants, landing in the same table the reporting and export paths read.
findings.recommendation: Never read org_id from the file: set it to upload.org_id unconditionally and drop the column from build_row. Validate each row before writing — build the Invoice objects and check valid?, or apply the same constraints explicitly — and if insert_all is needed for throughput, back it with database-level constraints (a NOT NULL and CHECK on amount_cents, an enum or CHECK on status and currency, a unique index on org_id and reference) so the fast path cannot write what the model forbids.

triage.reason: The model validations are the compensating control and insert_all is the documented bypass of them; no database constraints are declared anywhere in the tree (there is no schema.rb or migration directory) that would enforce the same invariants at the storage layer.
The values come from CSV.parse(upload.body) at :17, i.e. the uploaded document, and the class comment at :3-4 attributes that document to the partner.

The route and controller that create an Upload and enqueue this job are not in the tree — config/routes.rb declares no uploads resource, and there is no Upload model file — so I cannot establish from what I was given that a partner can actually trigger it, or what validation that entry point might apply first. This caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: the upload controller and its route. The two defects in this file are certain regardless of who triggers it.

findings.title: Credit postings are written with update_columns, which skips every validation on the amount and deliberately freezes the timestamp the audit feed watches
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: credit! writes with update_columns
findings.evidence: credit! writes `@invoice.update_columns(amount_cents: @invoice.amount_cents - amount_cents, updated_at: @invoice.updated_at)` at :32-35. update_columns issues a direct UPDATE, running no validations and no callbacks, so three model rules are skipped on the one path that changes an invoice's amount: `validates :amount_cents, numericality: { only_integer: true, greater_than: 0 }` (invoice.rb:9), the before_save assert_ledger_balanced (:15, :39-47) whose comment at :37-38 says the row must agree with its ledger entries or the month-end trial balance drifts, and stamp_posted_at (:14). The caller supplies the amount as `Integer(adjustment_params[:amount_cents])` (adjustments_controller.rb:22), which accepts a negative or arbitrarily large value — Integer() rejects non-numerics but constrains neither sign nor magnitude. The second argument is the audit half: updated_at is explicitly reassigned to its existing value, and the comment at :26-28 states the intent, to keep the change off the updated_at churn the audit feed subscribes to.
findings.impact: An adjustment can drive an invoice's amount_cents below zero or to a value that contradicts its ledger entries, and the model rule written to prevent exactly that drift never executes. Because the amount may be negative, a 'credit' can also increase what is owed. The frozen updated_at means the change does not appear to any consumer that watches that column — so the record moves and the audit feed does not see it, which turns an integrity bug into one that resists detection. Via LA-01 and LA-02, the caller need be neither an admin nor the invoice's owner.
findings.recommendation: Validate the amount at the controller boundary — positive, integer, and not exceeding the invoice's outstanding balance — and write through update! so the model's own invariants run. If the association-reload cost is the real concern, keep update_columns but re-assert assert_ledger_balanced explicitly afterwards and raise on failure. Remove the updated_at pinning: if the audit feed is too noisy, fix the feed's filter rather than hiding financial writes from it.

triage.reason: The model validations are the control and update_columns is the documented bypass. Nothing between adjustments_controller.rb:22 and ledger_posting.rb:32 bounds the amount: Integer() converts, and Adjustment.create! at :24 validates the Adjustment row, not the invoice arithmetic.

The bypass is intended in the narrow sense that the comment explains it, but nothing bounds it: the comment justifies avoiding updated_at churn and association reloads, neither of which requires skipping the amount validation or the balance assertion.

Not an absent defence beside a working one. assert_ledger_balanced is the only place the invariant is checked and there are no database constraints in the tree, so the impact — a ledger row that disagrees with its entries, unseen by the audit feed — reaches the user.

findings.title: Ledger fields are written into the export CSV with no neutralisation of leading formula characters
findings.unaided_label: ledger-api: csv cells not neutralised
findings.evidence: `rows.each { |invoice| csv << HEADERS.map { |h| invoice.public_send(h) } }` at :42 writes each field verbatim. Two of the six columns in HEADERS (:37) are free text an ordinary partner sets — reference and memo, both in invoice_params at invoices_controller.rb:53 — and neither is checked for a leading '=', '+', '-', '@', tab or carriage return anywhere in the write path. The response is served as text/csv with a .csv filename (:22-24), and the endpoint's own comment at :12-13 says the file is pulled so finance can open it in their spreadsheet template, which names the consumer that interprets those characters as a formula. The public_send at :42 is itself safe: it iterates the frozen HEADERS constant, not user input.
findings.impact: A partner sets an invoice memo to a spreadsheet formula and it executes when a member of the finance team opens the export. In Excel that reaches DDE and external references — data exfiltration to a remote host through a hyperlink or WEBSERVICE call, and in unpatched configurations command execution — with the payload arriving inside a file the recipient trusts because their own system produced it. Severity is low because it needs a human to open the file and to accept the spreadsheet's warning prompt.
findings.recommendation: Prefix any cell whose first character is '=', '+', '-', '@', tab or CR with a single quote, or wrap the value so the spreadsheet reads it as text, applied centrally in to_csv so every column is covered rather than the two that are risky today. Validate reference and memo at the write boundary as well.

triage.reason: reference and memo are permitted attributes on invoice create and update (invoices_controller.rb:52-54), so a partner writes them directly, and the export re-emits them unchanged.

The sink is dangerous in the form it is reached: the response is served as text/csv with a .csv filename (:22-24) and the comment at :12-13 identifies a spreadsheet as the consumer. A spreadsheet evaluates a leading '=' rather than displaying it.

There is no server-side equivalent control elsewhere that this duplicates — no escaping is applied at write time or read time. The severity is low on its own merits, because exploitation requires the recipient to open the file and dismiss a warning.

findings.title: The publication queue is exempted from every authorization decision because its path starts with the public register's prefix, and it defaults to including embargoed rows
findings.class: authorization bypass through an unbounded prefix match
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: publications matches the public prefix
findings.evidence: The filter computes `path = "/" + ctx.getUriInfo().getPath()` at :44 and returns without a decision when any entry in PUBLIC_PREFIXES is a prefix of it (:46-48). One entry is "/api/grants/public" (:29), intended for GrantResource.publicRegister, whose @Path is "public/register" under the class-level "/api/grants" (:86-90) — giving /api/grants/public/register. But GrantResource also declares @Path("publications") at :79, giving /api/grants/publications — and "/api/grants/publications".startsWith("/api/grants/public") is true, because the match has no segment boundary. So the publications endpoint skips the OPA call entirely. What it returns is the other half: its includeEmbargoed parameter is annotated @DefaultValue("true") at :81, so the default with no query string at all is the inclusive one, and repo.publications(true) drops the embargo predicate from the query (GrantRepository.java:42-44), returning every approved grant regardless of embargoedUntil. The doc comment at :73-77 states what that set contains: the rows comms stages ahead of an announcement, with the internal award notes attached.
findings.impact: GET /api/grants/publications, with no credential and no parameters, returns up to a thousand approved grants including every embargoed row — the awards not yet announced, together with the fields the projection carries (GrantRepository.java:23-25): reference, title, amount, department and status. That is unannounced funding decisions and their amounts, disclosed to anyone who can reach the service, and the exposure is a single unauthenticated GET rather than a chain. The public register beside it does the same query correctly with includeEmbargoed false.
findings.recommendation: Compare against a path segment boundary rather than a bare prefix — test equality against the exact public paths, or require the prefix to be followed by '/' or end-of-string — so a sibling resource cannot inherit an exemption by sharing an initial substring. Independently, change the @DefaultValue on includeEmbargoed to "false" so the safe reading is the default, and gate the inclusive branch on an explicit entitlement rather than on a query parameter the caller supplies.

triage.reason: The OPA decision is the only authorization layer and this path is what skips it: the return at :47 precedes the inputFor and evaluate calls at :50-54. GrantResource carries @Authorized at :28, which binds the filter to the class, but the filter's own first action is the exemption test.

The exposure is not the intended one: the comment at :24-27 lists what is meant to be reachable without a decision — the public grant register, the health probes and the OpenAPI document — and the publication queue with embargoed rows is none of those. The resource's own comment at :73-77 describes it as an internal staging view.

This is FP-11 inverted. The construct reads as an exemption for one public register and applies to strictly more than that, because startsWith admits any longer path sharing the prefix. It is wider than it looks, not narrower.

findings.title: The authorization filter is configured to permit the request when the policy sidecar cannot be reached, on a 400 millisecond timeout
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: on-error=permit
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter wraps the decision call in a catch-all — `catch (Exception e)` at :55 — and substitutes `OpaClient.Decision.onError(onError)` at :57, where onError is injected from grants.authz.on-error with a code default of "deny" (:39-40). The properties file overrides that default to permit at :15, and Decision.onError returns `new Decision(true, "policy sidecar unavailable, permitted")` for that value (OpaClient.java:49-51). The filter then takes the !decision.allow() branch at :60 and, being true, lets the request through. The window is narrow and attacker-influenceable: grants.opa.timeout is PT0.4S (:10, OpaClient.java:36) and the client connect timeout is 300ms (OpaClient.java:44), so any latency spike past 400 milliseconds on the sidecar turns into a permit rather than a denial. The comment at :12-14 gives the reason — the sidecar restarts on every bundle publish and rejecting during a roll took the caseworker UI down twice — so availability was traded for the access control, deliberately and in the production properties file.
findings.impact: Every authorization decision in the service becomes advisory. During a bundle publish, a sidecar restart, a container OOM, a node under memory pressure, or simply a 400ms tail latency, every request is allowed regardless of department, role or action — including approve on a grant and write on any record. An attacker who can add load to the pod, or who simply retries during a deployment window, converts that into unauthorized approvals. The failure is logged at warn (:56) and otherwise invisible, and the permit is total rather than degraded.
findings.recommendation: Set grants.authz.on-error=deny and keep the code default as it already is. Solve the availability problem where it belongs: run two sidecar replicas or use OPA's bundle hot-reload so a publish does not restart the process, cache the last good decision per principal for a short window and serve that on error instead of a blanket permit, and raise the timeout above the sidecar's real p99. Narrow the catch at :55 so a programming error in inputFor is not silently converted into a permit alongside genuine transport failures.

triage.reason: There is no second authorization layer to fall back on. The resources carry no @RolesAllowed or @PreAuthorize — GrantResource's methods (:44-90) declare only JAX-RS annotations — so when the filter permits, nothing else checks.

The value is in src/main/resources/application.properties, the production configuration compiled into the artifact, not in an application-dev.properties or a test profile. Quarkus profile-specific keys are prefixed with %dev or %test and this key is not.

Nothing narrows it: the catch at :55 covers every exception from evaluate, and the onError substitution applies to every request on every @Authorized resource, with no path, method or principal condition.

findings.title: A principal whose department is unknown or absent falls back to a baseline entitlement that grants more than any real department holds
findings.class: permissive default in an access-control policy
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: unknown dept gets the widest grants
findings.evidence: `entitlements := object.get(data.roles, input.user.dept, data.roles.baseline)` — the third argument is the value returned when the key is missing. roles.json:3-6 defines baseline with grants ["read", "write", "approve", "export"]: all four actions, which is strictly more than every named department in the same file — programmes has three (:9), finance two (:13), legal two (:25), comms and it one each (:17, :21). So the fallback for an unrecognised key is the most privileged entry in the table, and the allow rule at :13-16 grants any action found in it. The key itself is soft: OpaClient.inputFor puts `identity.<String>getAttribute("dept")` into the document at :82, and that returns null when the attribute is absent, so an identity with no dept — an unmapped directory entry, a service account, a token issued before the attribute existed — lands on the fallback rather than being denied. The comment at :8-10 states the intent, cost centres created after the last bundle build getting the shared baseline rather than being locked out on their first day.
findings.impact: Any principal the entitlement matrix does not recognise silently receives read, write, approve and export on grants — including approve, which the policy otherwise gates behind the grants.approver role at :27-30, and export, which finance and legal hold but programmes does not. A caseworker in a department that has not been added to the bundle can approve grant awards. The failure direction is the opposite of what an access-control default should be, and it is invisible: the decision is allow, so nothing is logged as denied and no one notices the department was never mapped.
findings.recommendation: Make the fallback empty rather than permissive — `object.get(data.roles, input.user.dept, {"grants": []})` — so an unmapped department is denied and the gap surfaces as a support ticket rather than as silent over-permission. If a genuine first-day baseline is needed, give it read only and nothing else. Separately, deny explicitly when input.user.dept is null or absent, so a missing attribute is never treated as a lookup miss.

triage.reason: This policy is the compensating layer for the whole service — the resources carry no role annotations of their own — so there is nothing behind it. The approve rule at :27-30 is an additional grant path, not a restriction on this one; the two are independent allow rules and either suffices.

input.user.dept comes from the identity attribute at OpaClient.java:82. Even treating the directory as trusted, the value that triggers the fallback is any string absent from roles.json, which includes null — and the set of mapped departments is a six-entry list that any new or renamed cost centre falls outside of.

There is no narrowing condition. object.get's default argument is returned unconditionally on a miss, and the allow rule at :13-16 iterates the resulting grants with no further predicate on the department.

findings.title: The attachments resource carries no @Authorized annotation, so the name-bound authorization filter never runs for it at all
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: AttachmentResource has no @Authorized
findings.from_tool: confirmed by symbol enumeration — grep for @Authorized across the tree returns exactly three hits: the annotation definition (Authorized.java:17), the filter that binds to it (AuthzFilter.java:18) and GrantResource (:28)
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter is a @NameBinding-scoped provider: it is annotated @Authorized at :18, and Authorized.java:14 declares @NameBinding, which means JAX-RS applies the filter only to resources or methods carrying the same annotation. GrantResource has it at :28. AttachmentResource, declared at :31-33 with @Path("/api/attachments"), does not — its class declaration is `@Path("/api/attachments") @Produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON) public class AttachmentResource`, and neither of its methods carries it either (:41-44, :62-65). So both endpoints run with no policy decision whatsoever: no OPA call, no entitlement lookup, no role check, and not even the PUBLIC_PREFIXES exemption, because the filter is never invoked to reach it. The class comment at :27-30 describes the contents as the signed award letter, the due diligence pack and the case-management manifest.
findings.impact: GET /api/attachments/{grantId}/{name} serves any attachment for any grant to any caller — signed award letters and due-diligence packs, which are exactly the sensitive documents in this system — with no authentication and no authorization, and grantId is a long that enumerates. POST /api/attachments/{grantId}/manifest accepts an XML document from anyone, which is what makes GP-05 reachable pre-authentication. The omission is a single missing annotation on a class beside one that has it, which is why it survives a review looking for a wrongly-configured filter.
findings.recommendation: Add @Authorized to AttachmentResource. Then remove the failure mode rather than fixing the instance: make the filter global — drop the @NameBinding and register it as a plain @Provider that denies by default — with an explicit, short allowlist of exempt paths, so a resource is protected unless someone deliberately exempts it. Add a test that walks the deployed resource classes and asserts each is either annotated or on the allowlist.

triage.reason: There is no other control on the class: no @RolesAllowed, no @Authenticated, no programmatic SecurityIdentity check in either method body, and application.properties declares no quarkus.http.auth.permission rules that would cover the path — the file was enumerated key by key and contains no auth keys at all.
The resource ships: it is a plain @Path-annotated CDI bean in src/main/java with no profile guard or conditional registration.

The benign reading would be that AuthzFilter is a global @Provider applying to every resource. It is not: it carries @Authorized at :18, and Authorized.java:14 is @NameBinding, which is precisely the JAX-RS mechanism that restricts a filter to annotated targets.

findings.title: The manifest endpoint parses caller-supplied XML with a DocumentBuilderFactory left at its default, which resolves external entities
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: manifest parser resolves external entities
findings.evidence: The method builds the factory at :66 and sets exactly three properties: setNamespaceAware(true) at :67, setIgnoringComments(true) at :68, setCoalescing(true) at :69. None of them concerns entity resolution. The hardening calls that would — setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true), disabling external-general-entities and external-parameter-entities, setXIncludeAware(false), setExpandEntityReferences(false), or FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING — are absent, and grep for setFeature and XMLConstants across the tree returns nothing. JAXP's default configuration resolves external entities, so `builder.parse(body)` at :72 processes a DOCTYPE and its entity declarations against a body taken straight from the request (:65). The result is walked at :74-80 and the resolved attribute values are echoed back in the response at :83, giving a direct read-back channel rather than a blind one.
findings.impact: A caller posts a manifest declaring an external entity and the service resolves it from its own network position: local files readable by the process — application.properties with the datasource URL, container secrets, /etc/passwd — returned in the indexed array of the response, and outbound requests to internal addresses, which is SSRF from inside the pod that also reaches the OPA sidecar on 127.0.0.1:8181. Because GP-04 leaves this resource with no authorization at all, none of that requires a credential. Entity expansion also gives a denial-of-service path against a service whose max body size is 32M (application.properties:3).
findings.recommendation: Disallow DOCTYPE declarations outright — factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true) — which is the single setting that closes the class for a document type that has no legitimate use for one. Add setXIncludeAware(false) and setExpandEntityReferences(false) as defence in depth, and set an EntityResolver that returns an empty source. Build the factory once in a hardened helper used by every parser in the codebase rather than configuring it at each call site.

triage.reason: Nothing sits in front of the parse: the body is the raw InputStream method parameter (:65) and reaches builder.parse at :72 with no schema validation, no pre-scan and no wrapper. There is no Quarkus-level XML hardening in application.properties, which was enumerated key by key.
The parsed document is the request body of a @Consumes(APPLICATION_XML) POST endpoint (:62-65) — entirely caller-controlled, and per GP-04 by a caller who needs no credential.

The sink is dangerous in the form reached: DocumentBuilder.parse with default JAXP settings performs entity resolution, and the sanitize call at :79 is applied to the resolved attribute value afterwards, which neither prevents the resolution nor stops the value being echoed at :83.

findings.title: The Kafka consumer writes grant records through the repository without any of the validation the REST payload enforces
findings.class: a validated entity written from a second, unvalidated path
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: kafka consumer writes past the REST validation
findings.evidence: GrantEntity has two writers. The REST path constrains its input with bean validation: GrantPayload declares @NotBlank @Size(max=64) on reference, @NotBlank @Size(max=240) on title, @NotNull @DecimalMin("0.00") @DecimalMax("5000000.00") on amount, @NotBlank @Size(max=32) on dept and @Pattern(regexp = "DRAFT|SUBMITTED|APPROVED|REJECTED") on status (GrantResource.java:36-42), and both create and update take it as @Valid (:51, :62). The consumer at GrantEventConsumer.java:43-47 calls the same repository with values pulled straight from the JsonObject: `new BigDecimal(grant.getString("amount", "0"))`, `grant.getString("dept", "programmes")` and `grant.getString("status", "DRAFT")`. There is no @Valid, no DTO, no pattern check and no range check — the only guard in the method is the reference blank test at :38-41. repo.applyEvent then writes amount, dept and status onto the row matched by reference (GrantRepository.java:89-96). The class comment at :13-18 states the design assumption directly: the payload is the same record shape the REST endpoint takes.
findings.impact: Anyone able to publish to grants.events.v2 sets a grant's status to APPROVED without passing the approve action the policy gates behind the grants.approver role (authz.rego:27-30), and sets its amount above the five-million ceiling the REST path enforces, or negative. That is the approval workflow bypassed by writing to a topic instead of calling the API. The dept field is equally free, and since GP-03 shows the policy keys entitlements on dept, writing an unmapped department onto a record is itself consequential. Separately, `new BigDecimal` on an unparseable string throws NumberFormatException inside a @Blocking @Transactional consumer with auto.offset.reset=earliest (application.properties:26), so one malformed message is a poison pill that stalls the partition.
findings.recommendation: Validate on the consumer as strictly as on the resource: deserialise into the same GrantPayload record and run the validator programmatically, rejecting the message to a dead-letter topic on failure rather than throwing. Do not accept status transitions from the topic at all if approval is meant to be a workflow action — apply amount and dept and leave status to the approve path. Wrap the BigDecimal parse so a malformed value is a rejected message rather than a stalled partition, and authenticate and authorise producers on the topic.

triage.reason: The repository applies no validation of its own: applyEvent (GrantRepository.java:89-96) binds the parameters into a JPQL update with no checks, and there is no @Valid on the method, no entity-level constraint annotation, and no database CHECK constraint declared anywhere in the tree.

The values come from the Kafka message body, deserialised as a raw JsonObject (application.properties:27) with no schema. Treating the topic as trusted would require an authorization boundary on it, and none is configured — the incoming channel declares connector, topic, group, offset and deserializer only.

The benign reading would be that the two writers do not reach the same effect. They do: both end in an update of amount, dept and status on a GrantEntity row, one through GrantRepository.update and one through GrantRepository.applyEvent, differing only in whether the row is matched by id or by reference.

findings.title: The shipped policy bundle contains an unconditional bypass rule keyed on a single input field
findings.class: debug bypass in a production access-control policy
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: debug_bypass clause in the bundle
findings.evidence: `allow if { input.debug_bypass == true }` at :34-36 — a complete allow rule with no other condition: no environment check, no principal check, no action or resource predicate. Rego's allow rules are disjunctive, so this one grants unconditionally whenever the field is true, regardless of what the four rules above it decide. The comment at :32-33 describes it as retained for the policy playground, loaded into a scratch OPA when someone is stepping through a decision by hand — but the clause is in policy/authz.rego, the same file that defines the real rules and that the service evaluates via grants.opa.decision-path (application.properties:9), not in a separate development bundle.
findings.impact: Any caller who can put debug_bypass into the decision document is authorized for everything. The service's own filter cannot be tricked into it — see the triage below — so the exposure is to any other client of the sidecar's decision API, and to the bundle being deployed to an OPA whose input is assembled by something other than this filter. It is also a standing hazard rather than an inert one: a future field added to inputFor, a switch to passing the request body through, or a second service adopting the bundle turns it live, and nothing in the policy would signal the change.
findings.recommendation: Delete the rule from the shipped bundle. If a playground bypass is genuinely useful, keep it in a separate .rego file that is only loaded into the scratch OPA, and add a bundle-build check that fails if the production bundle contains a rule referencing debug_bypass — the class is one a test can hold shut permanently, which is worth more than removing this instance.

triage.reason: No layer compensates inside the policy: the rule is an independent allow, and Rego evaluates the disjunction, so no other clause can veto it. The default allow := false at :6 applies only when no rule matches.

Whether an attacker can set the field depends on who else calls the decision API. From this service they cannot: OpaClient.inputFor builds the document field by field at :79-93 — user, resource, action — and never copies the request body or unknown fields, which its own comment at :75-78 states as the design. But the sidecar's decision API accepts input from any client that can reach it, and I cannot enumerate those from this tree. That is what caps this finding at probable. What would settle it: the pod definition and any other client of grants.opa.decision-path.

The clause is in the production policy file, not in a test fixture or a dev-only bundle. policy/authz.rego is the single policy source in the tree and application.properties:9 points the service at the package it defines.

findings.title: The auditor allow rule is keyed on a path prefix that no route in the service serves, so the cross-department read it grants can never fire
findings.class: an authorization rule that cannot take effect
findings.unaided_label: grant-policy: auditor clause names a path nothing serves
findings.from_tool: path_coverage.py — DEAD GUARD '/api/grants/audit' guards nothing: no route starts with it [grant-policy/policy/authz.rego:23]
findings.evidence: The rule at :20-24 grants read to a caller holding the auditor role when the resource path starts with "/api/grants/audit/". Joining that against the routes the service actually registers, no such path exists: GrantResource declares the class path /api/grants (:27) and four method paths — none, {id}, {id}/approve, publications and public/register (:44-90) — and AttachmentResource serves /api/attachments (:31). path_coverage.py, run over the tree, reported the same conclusion mechanically as its single DEAD GUARD across 42 route paths. The path the rule tests comes from OpaClient.inputFor at :86, which sets resource.path from the request URI, so the value is real; there is simply no request that can produce a match.
findings.impact: Not an exposure but a control that cannot fire, and the consequence is displaced rather than absent. Programme auditors, whom the comment at :18-19 describes as needing to read the audit trail across every department including grants their own cost centre never raised, get nothing from this rule — so in practice their access has to come from their department's entitlement instead, which is the row in roles.json that grants far more than read. A dead grant rule quietly pushes the requirement onto a broader one. It is also drift evidence: policy and routes have diverged, and nothing in the build notices.
findings.recommendation: Reconcile the two. Either implement the audit route the policy anticipates and keep the rule, or delete the rule and grant auditors their cross-department read through an explicit role entry rather than through a department entitlement. Then add the join to CI — the check that every path prefix named in the policy corresponds to a registered route, and that every registered route is reachable by some rule — so the next divergence fails a build instead of sitting in the bundle.

triage.reason: The audit route may exist in a module outside the tree I was given: the service ships two resource classes and a real deployment could register more, and the policy bundle is plainly written against a wider surface. I cannot establish absence from a partial scope, which caps this at probable. What would settle it: the full list of JAX-RS resources in the deployed artifact. The rule is reported rather than dropped because a policy clause and its routes are the join nobody runs, and the bound is stated here rather than assumed away.

FP-10 would apply if a working equivalent existed elsewhere and this were redundant depth. The opposite holds: no other rule grants an auditor a cross-department read, so the requirement falls back onto the department entitlement, which is wider. Severity is low because the direction of the failure is restrictive rather than permissive.
This rule asks whether a wide-looking construct applies to less than it appears to. Here the construct applies to nothing at all, which is the finding rather than an exculpation of it.
